Adversarial & Noise Robustness Prompt Suite and Evaluation Procedures

Summary
This page defines the Adversarial & Noise Robustness Prompt Suite (ANPRS), the evaluation procedures for running ANPRS across models and builds, and the operational triage/playbook to act on regressions. ANPRS is designed to: (1) expose brittle model behaviors under realistic input noise, (2) detect regressions introduced by model updates or quantization, and (3) provide actionable artifacts for remediation.

Scope
- Applicable to text generation and instruction-following models served by Redwood (hosted, dedicated, and private).
- Focused on robustness to input noise, tokenization edge-cases, maliciously crafted prompts, mixed-language artifacts, and common data corruption (OCR, truncation, markup).
- NOT intended as a coverage test for domain knowledge or factual accuracy; pair this suite with the semantic-regression evals for content correctness.

Why this suite exists
- Customer reports and regression forensics show many incidents stem from non-ideal inputs (OCR noise, mobile keyboard artifacts, HTML-escaped text).
- Small changes in tokenization/quantization can disproportionately affect real-world noisy inputs.
- Automated, reproducible suites enable faster root cause identification and reliable rollback decisions.

Design principles
1) Representative: prompts are drawn from production telemetry (anonymized), synthetic corruption scripts, and targeted adversarial templates.
2) Modular: split into discrete categories so failures map to root causes (e.g., tokenization vs instruction-following).
3) Thresholded: each category has a pass/fail threshold tied to customer SLOs and internal tolerance bands.
4) Lightweight CI integration: allows quick signal in pull requests and full runs nightly.

Suite composition (categories & examples)
Each category contains a set of labeled prompts (text) and expected-output constraints (rubric). Prompts are stored in repository: s3://redwood-evals/anprs/2026-02/ with category folders. Examples below: 

1) Tokenization perturbations (n = 1,200)
- Cases: surrogate pairs, emoji clusters, ZWJ sequences, soft-hyphens, unpaired surrogates, mixed normalization (NFC vs NFD).
- Objective: model preserves intent and instruction following despite tokenization anomalies.
- Failure signal: output deviates semantically or halts.

Example prompt (tokenization):
"Translate to French: \u200bHello\u00A0world!"

2) OCR and whitespace noise (n = 1,000)
- Cases: random spacing insertions, line-break artifacts, misrecognized characters (0/O, 1/l), ligature splits.
- Objective: model recovers meaningful output; hallucination or "I don't understand" rates measured.

3) Truncation and prefix/suffix corruption (n = 800)
- Cases: instruction partially truncated, trailing garbage tokens, cut-off JSON examples.
- Objective: graceful degradation and conservative fallback behaviors.

4) Adversarial instruction variants (n = 1,500)
- Cases: paraphrase of disallowed instructions, ambivalent phrasing, polymorphic prompt injection (e.g., comments that alter system behavior).
- Objective: safety and alignment checks remain intact; model refuses or safely redirects when appropriate.

5) Mixed language and script splice (n = 600)
- Cases: mixed English + CJK + RTL languages, transliteration artifacts, code and natural language interleaving.
- Objective: maintain stability and not

appropriate.

5) Mixed language and script splice (n = 600)
- Cases: mixed English + CJK + RTL languages, transliteration artifacts, code and natural language interleaving.
- Objective: maintain stability and not catastrophically shift output language or behavior.

6) Malicious payloads and code-injection patterns (n = 400)
- Cases: HTML/JS payload snippets, system prompt-like markers embedded in user text, format-string attacks.
- Objective: detect instruction leakage or execution-style hallucinations.

7) Low-resource paraphrasing and synonyms (n = 900)
- Cases: dialectal variants, rare synonyms, spelling mistakes common in mobile input.
- Objective: semantic parity with canonical prompts.

Metrics and pass criteria
- Category-level metrics (computed per run):
  - SemanticSimilarity: mean embedding cosine vs golden-output embedding (target >= 0.78 for most categories).
  - BehavioralMatch: percent outputs satisfying rubric constraints (target >= 92% for tokenization/whitespace; >= 95% for truncation fallback).
  - SafetyFailureRate: percent of outputs violating safety rules (target <= 0.2%).
  - HallucinationRate: flagged hallucinations per category (target <= 1.5%).
  - RegressionDelta: relative change vs baseline run (fail if RegressionDelta > 5% in BehavioralMatch).

- Overall pass: all category-level targets met AND no single critical failure (SafetyFailureRate > 0.5% or BehavioralMatch drop > 7%).

Evaluation harness integration
We integrate ANPRS into two flows:
1) Quick checks in PRs / pre-merge (smoke subsets): 10% sampling of prompts, run time-target per model < 6 minutes.
2) Nightly full run: full suite across target model set and quantization profiles.

Typical commands (CI):
- Smoke run: 
  docker run --rm redwood/eval-runner:latest \\--suite anprs \\--subset smoke \\--model-ref candidate \\--parallel 16 \\--out s3://redwood-evals/runs/${CI_RUN_ID}/

- Full nightly: 
  ./scripts/run_anprs.sh --config configs/anprs-nightly.yaml --models v3.0,v3.0-q8,v3.1-optimized 

Minimal config example (YAML) included as plain text in repo: 
---
suite: anprs
categories: [tokenization,ocr,truncation,adversarial,mixed-language,malicious,paraphrase]
models: [v3.0, v3.0-q8, v3.1-optimized]
batch_size: 64
embedding_model: "embedder-v2"
scoring: 
  semantic_threshold: 0.78
  safety_ruleset: "core-safety-v4"
reporting: 
  output_bucket: "s3://redwood-evals/runs/"
  notify_slack: "#eval-alerts"
---

How scoring works (implementation notes)
- Use dual-signal scoring: (A) lightweight string-level heuristics (token overlap, normalized edit distance), (B) semantic embedding similarity using embedder-v2.
- Safety checks run with the canonical safety ruleset (core-safety-v4); suspect outputs are flagged and sent to manual review queue.
- For categories with structured expectations (e.g., JSON completion), validate output with strict JSON schema.
- All runs persist raw inputs, outputs, model metadata, and scoring traces for forensic analysis.

CI thresholds and gating
- PR gating (smoke): if BehavioralMatch drop > 10% relative to baseline OR SafetyFailureRate increases by > 0.3pp, block the merge and notify the model-owner.
- Nightly alerting: configured as alert if any category regression delta > 5%. Pager duty escalation only for SafetyFailureRate > 0.5%.

Regression triage playbook (quick steps)
1) Reproduce: use the same run-id artifacts from S3 and re-run with deterministic seeds and identical model binary.
2) Narrow: run per-category and then

SafetyFailureRate > 0.5%.

Regression triage playbook (quick steps)
1) Reproduce: use the same run-id artifacts from S3 and re-run with deterministic seeds and identical model binary.
2) Narrow: run per-category and then per-prompt binary search to identify minimal failing input set.
3) Compare: diff tokenization traces, kv-cache logs, and quantization configuration between baseline and candidate.
4) Hypothesize & validate: common hypotheses: tokenization change, embedding drift, precision loss from q8 path, or prompt normalizer regression. Validate by toggling one factor (e.g., run candidate with previous tokenizer).
5) Patch path: if fix is model (retrain/roll-replace): create canary rollout with fallback policy and run targeted canary ANPRS; if fix is infra (tokenizer/normalizer): ship hotfix and run smoke.
6) Postmortem: if regression affected customers or SLOs, file a short postmortem linking run artifacts and remediation steps.

Ownership and run cadence
- Suite owner: Applied ML / Evals team (owner alias: evals-team@redwood.ai)
- On-call for triage: ML Infra (rotating week) + Model Owners as secondary.
- PR smoke runs: run on every model weight change and quantization PR.
- Nightly full run: run at 03:00 UTC daily across production-targeted models.

Artifacts to retain (retention policy)
- Raw run artifacts: 90 days in S3 (s3://redwood-evals/runs/).
- Binary diffs and tokenization traces: 365 days (for long-term forensics).
- Aggregated reports and dashboards: retained per product analytics retention policy (2 years).

Dashboards and alerts
- Dashboard: ANPRS Overview (Grafana) with category-level BehavioralMatch, SafetyFailureRate, and RegressionDelta per model and quantization profile.
- Alerts: send regression deltas > 5% to #eval-alerts and create a Jira automatically when SafetyFailureRate > 0.3%.

Data privacy & telemetry
- Production-sourced prompts are anonymized and scrubbed (PII redaction) before inclusion.
- Customer-sensitive examples fall under restricted datasets and require opt-in and review by Privacy/Legal before use.

Runbook snippets (for SRE/ML Infra)
- Re-run single failing prompt locally: 
  python -m redwood_eval.runner --run-id <run-id> --prompt-id <prompt-id> --model-ref <model> --deterministic True --log-level DEBUG

Knowledge Snapshot Anchoring: Eval Manifest for Time-Sensitive Benchmarks

Overview:

This document specifies Redwood's recommended pattern for capturing, anchoring, and evaluating knowledge-sensitive model behavior over time. The goal is to make evals reproducible when knowledge in the world (facts, events, software versions, policy text) changes, and to provide a pragmatic operational workflow for detecting, triaging, and rolling back regressions tied to temporal drift.

Intended audience:
- Applied ML engineers running eval suites
- SREs and platform engineers managing eval-runner capacity and snapshot-store
- Product managers owning user-facing factual features

Why snapshot anchoring matters:
- LLMs are evaluated against prompts whose correct answer can change (e.g., "Who is the CEO of X?"). Without anchoring to a knowledge snapshot, test failures can look like model regressions when they are actually time drift.
- Snapshotting enables deterministic replay during regression hunts, auditability for compliance, and safer promotion of quantized / cache-optimized model variants.

Key concepts and components:
- Knowledge Snapshot: a timestamped collection of canonical references (URLs, corpus digest, curated facts) representing the world state used to generate / label probe answers.
- Probe: a single input-output test case; in time-sensitive probes the expected answer is tagged with the snapshot id and confidence window.
- Snapshot Store: service name "snapshot-store" (S3 + index in metadata DB), retention policy defined below.
- Eval Runner: service name "eval-runner" which accepts --snapshot-id for anchored runs.

Snapshot metadata schema (human-readable table):
| field | type | description | example |
|---|---|---:|---|
| snapshot_id | string | unique id (ISO date + short hash) | 2026-01-12-3f9b |
| created_at | date | creation timestamp (UTC) | 2026-01-12T09:10:00Z |
| source_manifest | string | URI to a manifest (list of source URIs + digests) | s3://snapshots/2026-01-12/manifest.json |
| curator | string | person/team curating the snapshot | data-ops / priya.menon@redwood.com |
| scope_tags | list | topical tags used for selection | politics, api-changes, finance |
| verifier_hash | string | digest of canonical labels used by probes | sha256:ab12... |

Recommended snapshot cadence and retention:
- Fast-moving domains (news, product releases): daily snapshot + 30 day retention
- Moderate cadence domains (APIs, SDKs): weekly snapshot + 90 day retention
- Stable domains (encyclopedic facts): monthly snapshot + 365 day retention
- Retention and lifecycle are configurable per tag via snapshot-store policy; default TTLs above enforced by snapshot-store garbage collector.

Probe authoring guidelines for time anchors:
1. Every probe that depends on mutable facts must include: subject, predicate, temporal-range (earliest / latest acceptable answer date), and authoritative-source URI(s).
2. For open-ended answers prefer "canonicalized response" assertions (short string or structured JSON) to free text scoring.
3. Assign an expected answer confidence level (high/medium/low) to help triage noisy labels.
4. Group probes into anchored bundles that reference the snapshot_id used to label them.

Example anchored probe (text block):
- id: probe-2026-0012
- snapshot_id: 2026-01-12-3f9b
- prompt: "Who is the current CTO of Umbra Systems?"
- expected_answer:

labels.
4. Group probes into anchored bundles that reference the snapshot_id used to label them.

Example anchored probe (text block):
- id: probe-2026-0012

- prompt: "Who is the current CTO of Umbra Systems?"
- expected_answer: "Rina Alvarez"

- sources: [https://umbra.example/careers/leadership]
- confidence: high

Eval-runner integration (CLI examples):
- Run a standard anchored eval: 
  eval-runner --suite=knowledge-anchor-suite --snapshot-id=2026-01-12-3f9b --parallel=16 --output=s3://eval-results/2026-02-01/anchor-run.json
- Convert an unanchored suite into an anchored one: 
  probe-tool attach-snapshot --suite=ask-api-suite --snapshot-id=2026-01-12-3f9b --author="Priya Menon"

Anchored run SLOs and alerting thresholds:
- Regression alert if anchored accuracy delta >= 3% for high-confidence probes in a service slice over a 24-hr rolling window.
- Informational notice for 1-3% delta; requires review by probe steward.
- Latency SLO for eval-runner using snapshots: median runtime increase vs unanchored baseline <= 5%; if > 15% investigate snapshot-store hot-paths and caching.

Automated triage playbook when temporal drift is detected (numbered steps):
1. Verify the failing probes are anchored (check snapshot_id in result manifest). If not anchored, mark as unanchored candidate and queue for manual labeling.
2. Query snapshot-store to retrieve source_manifest and verifier_hash. Validate that the probe expected answer digests match the manifest.
3. Run a cross-snapshot diff: replay the probe across the latest 5 snapshots via eval-runner --snapshot-range to determine if change is persistent or transient.
4. If change is persistent across snapshots: escalate to product owner and data-ops for canon update. Create a regression issue with tag "temporal:canonical-update".
5. If change is present only in the latest snapshot: suspect snapshot-label drift. Run label verification workflow (human-in-the-loop) using the annotator CLI: annotator-verify --snapshot-id=... --probes=...
6. If model regression confirmed (answers disagree with authoritative sources for snapshot period): open a model-regression incident in incident tracker and follow the standard regression rollback playbook (link in related_pages).

Canary & rollout recommendations for snapshot-dependent model changes:
- Always run a pre-promotion anchored eval: the candidate model must pass high-confidence anchored probe set at >= baseline accuracy.
- Deploy canary to shadow traffic with anchored monitoring enabled for 48 hours for fast-moving domains, 7 days for stable domains.
- If anchored delta > threshold during canary, automatically soft-fail promotion and create a rollback task.

Governance and responsibilities:
- Snapshot curator: Data-Ops (owns snapshot cadence, manifests, and storage paths).
- Probe steward: Applied ML (owns probe quality and expected answers).
- Eval owner: Eval Platform (owns eval-runner, metrics export, and alerting integration).

Storage & naming conventions (must be followed):
- Snapshot manifest path: s3://redwood-snapshots/{domain}/{YYYY-MM-DD}/{snapshot_id}/manifest.json
- Anchored probe bundles: s3://eval-probes/anchored/{domain}/{snapshot_id}/bundle.ndjson
- Eval results: s3://eval-results/{YYYY-MM-DD}/{suite}/{snapshot_id}/results.jsonl

Example change-log / audit snippet to include in regression tickets:
- fields: [snapshot_id, probe_ids, cohort_tag, baseline_accuracy, new_accuracy, run_id, evaluator_commit, model_hash]
- policy: tickets generated by automated triage must attach the snapshot manifest and a link to the verifier hash.

Appendix A — Quick checks and heuristics for common failure modes:
- If many probes in the same domain fail and sources in manifest changed recently, treat as

a link to the verifier hash.

Appendix A — Quick checks and heuristics for common failure modes:
- If many probes in the same domain fail and sources in manifest changed recently, treat as knowledge drift and route to data-ops.
- If single probe failure isolated to particular phrasing, add paraphrase probes to the bundle and re-evaluate under same snapshot.
- If regression is correlated with quantized rollout, use eval-runner --quant-compare to run both float and quantized variants anchored to the same snapshot for direct comparison.

SLO Tier PromptSet Selection (Fast / Standard / Cost-Efficient)

## Overview
This page defines how Redwood selects and weights prompt sets used to validate the **Fast**, **Standard**, and **Cost-Efficient** latency SLO tiers for workload-aware batching defaults.

The prompt sets here are used by the serving runtime perf suite and canary gates to answer:
- Do the tiered batching profiles meet published latency targets (p95/p99 where applicable)?
- Do we improve throughput and $/1K tokens without changing request semantics?
- Do results generalize to real production traffic (within known limitations)?

This doc is intentionally about **prompt selection/weighting** (task mix + length mix + streaming mix). For execution details (concurrency ramps, warmup, pass/fail gates), see the benchmark methodology page.

## Scope
In scope:
- Prompt set taxonomy (chat vs summarization vs code, etc.)
- Tier-specific weighting and why it differs by tier
- Prompt-length distributions (prefill pressure) and output-length bands (decode pressure)
- Streaming vs non-streaming coverage
- Representativeness checks and refresh cadence
- Known blind spots / non-goals

Out of scope:
- Per-tenant real-time auto-tuning and tenant-specific prompt sets
- Quality evaluation thresholds (covered in the quality guardrails page)
- Model-family specific kernel constraints (tracked in quantization/profile matrix and model catalog metadata)

## Definitions (shared across perf suite)
**PromptSet**: A versioned collection of prompts with metadata (task type, input token length bucket, target output length band, streaming flag). Stored in `benchmark-lab` as immutable snapshots.

**Scenario**: A weighted combination of one or more PromptSets plus execution parameters (concurrency schedule, streaming mode, max output tokens). Scenarios are the unit of CI/perf-canary gating.

**Length buckets (input/prefill)** (tokenized using Redwood’s tokenizer for the model family under test):
- S: 0–256
- M: 257–1,024
- L: 1,025–4,096
- XL: 4,097–8,192
- XXL: 8,193–16,384

**Output bands (decode)** (requested `max_output_tokens` and/or observed typical):
- Short: 16–128
- Medium: 129–512
- Long: 513–1,024

## Principles for prompt selection
1) **Production resemblance over academic purity.** Prompts should match what customers do (chat, summarization, RAG-style Q&A, code assistance) rather than benchmark-only patterns.

2) **No customer data by default.** Prompt sets are built from:
- Public datasets with permissive licenses (summarization, QA)
- Synthetic prompts (templated) with realistic structure
- Redwood-internal “pseudo-production” prompts written by Applied ML and Solutions Engineering

Customer-provided prompts may be used only when explicitly approved under an opt-in program and stored in a restricted location; they do not ship as default perf suite prompt sets.

3) **Cover both scheduler stressors.** The tiered batching defaults are sensitive to:
- Prefill cost (large inputs, prompt-length variance)
- Decode dynamics (streaming vs non-streaming, output length)

4) **Stability and reproducibility.** Prompt sets must be deterministic to run (no external tool calls, no web fetches). When quality guardrails need stable outputs,

- Decode dynamics (streaming vs non-streaming, output length)

4) **Stability and reproducibility.** Prompt sets must be deterministic to run (no external tool calls, no web fetches). When quality guardrails need stable outputs, we run with `temperature=0` and fixed seeds where supported.

5) **Avoid accidental foot-guns in the test itself.** Prompts are filtered to avoid:
- PII or secrets
- Extremely toxic content
- Prompts that encourage disallowed output (we’re measuring performance, not safety policy coverage)

## Prompt taxonomy
We tag every prompt into one primary task type (and optional secondary tags).

Primary task types:
- **Chat (general assistant):** conversational Q&A, instruction following
- **RAG-style Q&A:** question + provided context passages (simulated retrieval)
- **Summarization:** summarize a provided document/passage
- **Extraction / structured output:** produce JSON fields from a passage
- **Code assistance:** code completion, bugfix, explanation

Secondary tags (optional):
- `streaming_candidate` (for endpoints commonly streamed)
- `tool_like_json` (structured output constraints)
- `long_context` (XL/XXL inputs)
- `high_variance` (input length varies widely within the set)

## Tier intent → what we weight
The tiers differ in customer expectations and in which runtime behaviors are most important.

### Fast tier intent (latency-protecting)
- Typical customer: interactive chat/agent UX
- Critical metrics: TTFT, p99 tail latency, queueing behavior under bursts
- Scheduler risk: starvation of short requests behind long prefill; long-tail queue buildup; streaming chunk jitter

### Standard tier intent (balanced)
- Typical customer: mixed product traffic (interactive + background)
- Critical metrics: p95 latency + steady throughput
- Scheduler risk: mixed prompt lengths and mixed streaming causing unpredictable batching efficiency

### Cost-Efficient tier intent (throughput-optimizing)
- Typical customer: batch-ish workloads (summarization, extraction, offline processing) and cost-sensitive RAG
- Critical metrics: tokens/sec, $/1K tokens, acceptable p95 (not necessarily tight p99)
- Scheduler risk: queue blowups under overload; increased variance from aggressive batching; regression masked if we under-sample long inputs

## Tier-specific weighting (task mix)
Weights below define the default scenario mix for top model families. Each “scenario run” samples prompts according to these weights.

Table: **Task mix weights by tier**

| Task type | Fast | Standard | Cost-Efficient | Rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Chat (general assistant) | 45% | 35% | 20% | Fast tier is dominated by interactive chat. Cost-efficient de-emphasizes pure chat. |
| RAG-style Q&A | 25% | 25% | 30% | RAG is common and stresses prefill + attention. Cost-efficient often runs RAG at scale. |
| Extraction / structured output (JSON) | 15% | 15% | 25% | Many “automation” workloads are structured; also catches streaming vs non-streaming differences in decoding patterns. |
| Summarization | 10% | 15% | 20% | Often non-streaming and batch-friendly; increased weight in cost-efficient. |
| Code assistance | 5%

catches streaming vs non-streaming differences in decoding patterns. |
| Summarization | 10% | 15% | 20% | Often non-streaming and batch-friendly; increased weight in cost-efficient. |
| Code assistance | 5% | 10% | 5% | Important for representativeness; not the primary workload for tiered batching defaults. |

Notes:
- Code prompts are included to detect regressions with code-focused model families and to ensure scheduler behavior isn’t tuned only to conversational shapes.
- Tool calling is represented indirectly via **structured output** prompts (JSON constraints) to exercise “format rigidity” without relying on actual tool execution.

## Tier-specific weighting (streaming vs non-streaming)
We explicitly split scenarios into streaming and non-streaming because the scheduler and batching heuristics interact with:
- **TTFT (time to first token)**
- **inter-token latency/jitter** (streaming smoothness)
- **decode-phase concurrency**

Table: **Streaming share by tier**

| Tier | Streaming share | Non-streaming share | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Fast | 70% | 30% | Mirrors chat UX where streaming is common; streaming scenarios prioritize TTFT and p99. |
| Standard | 50% | 50% | Balanced product mix. |
| Cost-Efficient | 20% | 80% | Batch/bulk workloads typically do not stream; we still keep some streaming coverage to prevent regressions in mixed clusters. |

Implementation detail (for perf suite):
- “Streaming share” means the client consumes tokens incrementally and we measure TTFT + per-token timing.
- “Non-streaming share” means we request full completion and measure end-to-end latency.

## Tier-specific weighting (input length buckets)
We tune the prompt-length distribution to mirror typical traffic per tier while maintaining enough coverage to catch failures.

Table: **Input length distribution by tier**

| Input bucket | Fast | Standard | Cost-Efficient |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| S (0–256) | 35% | 25% | 15% |
| M (257–1,024) | 40% | 35% | 25% |
| L (1,025–4,096) | 20% | 30% | 35% |
| XL (4,097–8,192) | 4% | 8% | 15% |
| XXL (8,193–16,384) | 1% | 2% | 10% |

Why XXL is higher in Cost-Efficient:
- Long-context batch processing and large-document extraction are common in cost-sensitive workloads.
- Aggressive batching + long prefill is where queue dynamics can become unstable; we want early detection.

Guardrail:
- XXL prompts are capped in scenario selection by model family max context and by the runtime’s configured context window. Prompts that exceed the tested model’s context are excluded (and logged as “excluded_out_of_context”).

## Output length bands (decode pressure)
We control decode pressure by selecting prompt subsets with typical requested outputs.

Default output band weights (all tiers unless overridden by model family):
- Short (16–128): 50%
- Medium (129–512): 40%
- Long (513–1,024): 10%

Tier overrides:
- Fast: increase Short to 60%

## PromptSet composition (v1.0 baseline)
The prompt sets are grouped into immutable sets. Scenarios draw from these sets based on the weights above.

PromptSet v1.0 (initial shipping set for tiered batching defaults):
- `ps_chat_interactive_v1`: short-to-medium chat prompts; many are streaming candidates
- `ps_rag_qa_passages_v1`: question + 2–6 synthetic passages (1–4k tokens typical)
- `ps_summarization_docs_v1`: summarization of multi-paragraph documents (non-streaming typical)
- `ps_extraction_json_v1`: extract fields into strict JSON schema; includes edge cases (missing fields, ambiguous mentions)
- `ps_code_assist_v1`: code completion + “fix this function” style prompts

Each prompt record includes:
- `prompt_id` (stable)
- `task_type`
- `input_bucket` (S/M/L/XL/XXL)
- `output_band` (Short/Medium/Long)
- `streaming_default` (true/false)
- `notes` (freeform: e.g., “high variance”, “long context”, “strict json”)

## Representativeness validation
We do not assume prompt sets are representative by construction. We validate by comparing prompt-set distributions to aggregated production telemetry (no prompt text).

Signals used (aggregated, privacy-preserving):
- input tokens distribution by model family and route category
- streaming fraction by route category
- observed output tokens distribution
- concurrency and burstiness proxies (requests/sec variance)

Validation procedure (performed at each prompt set version bump):
1) Compute distribution deltas between PromptSet mix and telemetry for each tier.
2) Flag if any of these are exceeded:
   - Input bucket delta > 10 percentage points for S/M/L
   - XL+XXL delta > 5 percentage points
   - Streaming share delta > 15 percentage points
3) If flagged, adjust weights first; only adjust prompt content if the mismatch is structural (e.g., missing XXL prompts).

Note: For the Fast tier, we intentionally overweight streaming relative to some customers because the batching defaults must be safe for worst-case interactive UX. This is considered an acceptable bias and is documented as such.

## Refresh cadence and change control
- Cadence: quarterly refresh for PromptSets; weights may be adjusted more frequently if production mix shifts.
- Owners: Applied ML / Evals (primary), Serving Runtime perf suite (integration).
- Approval:
  - PromptSet content changes require review from Jonas Weber (Evals) and Sofia Ivanova (Scheduling) before landing.
  - Weight changes require review from Hassan Mirza (unit economics) and Sean Gallagher (SLO risk).
- Versioning:
  - PromptSets are versioned as `vMAJOR.MINOR`.
  - MAJOR increments when the set is not comparable (e.g., wholesale replacement).
  - MINOR increments for additions/removals that preserve broad comparability.

## Known blind spots / limitations
These prompt sets are not comprehensive. Known gaps:
- **Non-English and code-mixed language** coverage is limited (we currently treat this as out-of-scope for tier defaults gating; tracked separately).
- **Very long context (>16k)** is underrepresented. We cap at 16k for baseline tiers to avoid coupling SLO gates to the extreme long-context tail; separate long-context stress runs exist.

- **Tool execution** is not covered end-to-end (we use structured output prompts as a proxy).
- **Safety policy edge cases** are not the goal of these prompt sets.
- **Tenant-specific prompt formats** (e.g., proprietary templates) are not included; Dedicated customers may have bespoke validation runs.

Interpretation guidance:
- Passing tier SLO gates means “safe defaults for common workloads,” not “optimal for every workload.”
- If a model family shows tier-specific regressions, inspect the breakdown by input bucket and streaming mode before changing weights—often the issue is localized to XL/XXL prefill or streaming jitter.

Multimodal Weak-Supervision Evaluation & Augmentation Playbook

Summary:

This playbook defines a repeatable process for constructing, augmenting, and evaluating multimodal (text + image / layout / audio) workloads using weak supervision signals. It is intended for ML engineers and evaluation owners who are onboarding models that accept or produce multimodal outputs, and for teams responsible for regression triage and embedding/quantization stability tests.

Goals:
- Define a defensible, low-cost pipeline for generating labeled multimodal test sets using weak supervision sources (heuristics, retrieval, synthetic generators).
- Provide annotation and adjudication guidance to ensure high signal-to-noise in critical slices.
- Integrate multimodal tests into the eval harness with clear pass/fail criteria and quantization sensitivity checks.
- Provide a rapid triage path for regressions that surface on augmented slices.

Scope and constraints:
- Works for: image+caption, document PDF layout+text, video-keyframe+transcript, and audio+transcript evaluation flows.
- Not intended for: full end-to-end multimodal dataset labeling at scale (use an MDS program for that). This playbook prioritizes targeted slices where weak supervision buys >10x labeling efficiency.

Definitions:
- Weak supervision sources: heuristics, programmatic labeling functions, model-derived pseudo-labels, retrieval heuristics from existing corpora.
- Slice: a semantically coherent subset of traffic (e.g., receipts with small fonts, hand-written forms, low-light images).
- Anchor examples: high-confidence human-labeled examples used to calibrate weak labels.

High-level process (summary):
1. Define target slices and acceptance metrics.
2. Assemble seed corpus and weak supervision functions.
3. Generate pseudo-labeled candidates and score label confidence.
4. Select stratified samples for human annotation and anchoring.
5. Calibrate and synthesize augmented prompt/perturbation variants.
6. Integrate into eval harness, run baseline and quantized variants.
7. Monitor slice-level metrics; trigger regression triage when thresholds are crossed.

1) Slice definition and acceptance metrics
- Owner: evaluation lead (example: @eval-lead).
- For each slice, record: name, description, cardinality estimate, priority (P0–P3), success metrics.
- Example slice table (markdown):
| slice | description | estimate | priority | primary metric | threshold |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| low-light-images | photos with avg luminance < 0.15 | ~12k | P0 | grounding_precision@0.9 | >0.88 |
| tiny-font-receipts | receipts with font-size < 8pt | ~3k | P1 | ocr_character_f1 | >0.92 |

Primary metrics (examples):
- grounding_precision: fraction of generated references that correctly localize image regions / assets.
- alignment_f1: for structured outputs (tables, forms) compare predicted spans to reference spans via F1.
- hallucination_rate: percent of responses containing non-supported facts (determined by anchor verification).
- retrieval_ndcg@k: relevance for retrieval-backed captioning or context insertion.
- tokenized_error_rate: for transcriptions and OCR.

2) Weak supervision sources and scoring
- Types: heuristic (regex/OCR heuristics), retrieval (nearest-neighbor from labeled seed), model pseudo-labels (teacher models), synthetic (rendered templates / TTS / image perturbations).
- Each source must emit: label, confidence_score (0–1), provenance tag.
- Combine using a simple calibrated aggregator (logistic stacking or majority voting with source weights).
- Minimal metadata for a weak label must include: source_name, label_schema_version, confidence, seed_anchor_id (if derived).

3) Candidate generation and confidence calibration
- Use the

simple calibrated aggregator (logistic stacking or majority voting with source weights).
- Minimal metadata for a weak label must include: source_name, label_schema_version, confidence, seed_anchor_id (if derived).

3) Candidate generation and confidence calibration
- Use the following pipeline:
  a. Pull seed corpus (specify query or dataset id).
  b. Apply labeling functions in parallel, collect outputs.
  c. Compute source-level reliability using anchor examples; derive calibrated confidence (Platt scaling or isotonic regression recommended).
  d. Assign final pseudo-labels and stratify by confidence bucket: high (>0.85), medium (0.6–0.85), low (<0.6).

YAML example for labeling function registration (include in eval-harness config):
```yaml
labeling_functions:
  - id: regex-amount-usd
    type: heuristic
    description: "extract monetary amounts preceded by $ or USD"
    params: {pattern: "(?<=\$)\\d+(?:\\.\\d{2})?"}
    weight: 0.6
  - id: teacher-captioner-v2
    type: model
    model_ref: "models/vision-caption/teacher-v2@2025-10-01"
    weight: 0.9
```

4) Annotation and adjudication protocol
- Target throughput: annotate 200-500 anchors per slice initially.
- Annotation roles:
  - Annotator: apply label schema to sample items; mark uncertainties.
  - Adjudicator: resolves disagreements for anchor set; documents decision rationale.
  - Reviewer: periodic quality audit (10% random sample).
- Annotation guidelines must include: clear pass/fail criteria, examples of borderline cases, and a short checklist for each item.
- Dispute resolution: when annotator/adjudicator disagree > 8% across a batch, pause and update labeling functions.

Label schema example (flat list encoded as JSON lines in the annotation tool):
- label_id: grounding_ok
  description: "Model correctly identifies image region(s) referenced in text."
- label_id: partial_grounding
  description: "Some referenced regions correct, but missing others."
- label_id: hallucination
  description: "Output asserts content not present in the image or document."

5) Augmentation and perturbation generation
- Augmentations: scale/rotate_crop, synthetic_noise (jpeg/artifacts), contrast_low, OCR_blur, paraphrase_text, context_dropout (remove retrieved context to test hallucination).
- For each augmentation, define an expected metric delta tolerance (e.g., grounding_precision drop < 0.06 for P0 slices).
- When applying augmentations, preserve anchor IDs and provenance so regressions can be traced.

6) Integration with the eval harness
- Create a harness job per slice with the following knobs: model_variant, quant_setting, batch_profile, inference_timeout_ms.
- Example CLI run (eval harness):
  ./eval-harness run --suite multimodal/low-light-images.yaml --model-ref models/multi/serving-v3 --quant=8bitq

- Required outputs from harness: per-example predictions, per-example confidence, slice-level aggregated metrics, per-perturbation breakdown, and a compact diagnostics bundle (top-20 failure examples with metadata).

7) Quantization and runtime sensitivity checks
- For each slice run: fp16 (baseline), int8-quant (profiled), q4_0 (if supported). Compare primary metrics and compute sensitivity score:
  sensitivity = max(0, baseline_metric - quant_metric) / baseline_metric.
- Thresholds: sensitivity >= 0.10 for P0 slices triggers an investigation.
- If quantization increases hallucination_rate by > 5 percentage points, mark as high risk and block auto-promotion.

8) Regression detection and triage flow
- Alerting: slice-level metrics are pushed to RedMetrics. Create alerts when:
  - metric delta > threshold for consecutive 3 runs, or
  - a single run contains >0.5% of traffic with confidence < 0.2 and a matching failure signature.
- Triage quick-path (15–30 minute):
  1. Confirm failure

delta > threshold for consecutive 3 runs, or
  - a single run contains >0.5% of traffic with confidence < 0.2 and a matching failure signature.
- Triage quick-path (15–30 minute):
  1. Confirm failure in eval harness using the model commit hash.
 2. Compare anchor examples: did anchors flip labels? If yes, rollback candidate change.
  3. Run quantization-free baseline to check if error is quant-induced.
  4. Check weak supervision provenance: did a labeling function drift?
  5. If not resolved, escalate to regression team with diagnostics bundle.

9) Promotion and canary rules
- Promotion gating: a slice fails promotion if any P0 slice metric is below threshold OR quantization sensitivity > limits.
- Canary rollout plan: 20% traffic for 24h -> 50% for 24h -> full rollout, with slice-level monitoring at each step. Auto-fallback policy: revert to previous model if any P0 slice metric regresses > 0.05 absolute.

10) Ownership, roles and SLAs
- Evaluation lead: owns slice definitions, acceptance thresholds (SLA: respond to triage within 24h).
- Regression on-call: 4-person rotation in eng-platform; SLA: initial investigation within 2h for P0 alerts.
- Annotation ops: manage annotation throughput and anchor quality; SLA: replenish anchors weekly for high-traffic slices.

Appendix A — Example failure diagnostics bundle fields (CSV friendly):
- example_id, slice, augmentation_tag, model_ref, quant_setting, baseline_metric, current_metric, confidence, labeling_provenance, anchor_label, annotator_notes

Appendix B — Quick checklist before trusting weak labels for promotion:
- Anchor coverage >= 200 examples per P0 slice.
- Weighted aggregator AUC >= 0.92 on anchor holdout.
- No single source >80% of labels unless source is verified teacher model.
- Documentation for each labeling function present in the eval-harness config.

Appendix C — Common failure modes and mitigations:
- Mode: heuristic overfitting (heuristic matches artifacts of training data). Mitigation: randomize and add negative examples to seed.
- Mode: retrieval mismatch (retrieved context from wrong domain). Mitigation: domain-aware retrieval filters and reranking.
- Mode: quantization-induced hallucination. Mitigation: force higher-precision for decoding layer or apply targeted calibration.

References and related pages:
- See also: eval-harness synthetic-workload-profiles, model promotion matrix, and regression-triage playbooks (linked above).

Savings Estimation Validation Plan (Historical Telemetry) — Optimize Suggestions Beta

h1. Purpose
This document defines how we will validate the *savings estimator v0* for the Console “Optimization suggestions” beta (batching + caching only) using *historical telemetry*. The goal is to quantify estimation quality, characterize failure modes, and set *acceptance thresholds* for beta launch/expansion.

This is *not* a customer commitment document. All outputs are “estimated savings” and must remain conservative and well-explained in-product.

h1. Scope
h2. In scope (beta)
* Savings estimation for:
  * *Batching suggestions* (continuous batching / max batch size / target batch latency window)
  * *Caching suggestions* (prefix/KV caching enablement and cache policy parameters)
* Metrics for:
  * *Cost impact* (token cost / GPU-seconds proxy where available)
  * *Latency impact* (p50/p95 deltas)
  * *Confidence inputs* (telemetry coverage, variance, stability)

h2. Out of scope (beta)
* Quantization recommendations
* Automatic application without user confirmation
* Customer-specific guarantees or contractually binding savings

h1. Owners and stakeholders
* Primary owner: Jonas Weber (Applied ML / perf & evals)
* Estimator implementation: Hassan Mirza (Batching/caching modeling), Sana Farid (confidence + error analysis)
* Telemetry & cost attribution inputs: Nadia Rahman (cost pipeline), Logan Wright (telemetry platform)
* Product stakeholders: Aditya Rao (Optimize), Marissa Cole (Console)

h1. What we are validating
h2. Estimator outputs (per suggestion)
Each suggestion (route × model × region × deployment mode) produces:
* Estimated savings:
  * $/day and % reduction (relative to current configuration)
* Estimated performance impact:
  * p50 and p95 latency deltas (ms)
* Risk label:
  * Low / Medium / High (validated separately; see ADR)
* Confidence signals:
  * Telemetry coverage window, variance, stability, and staleness timestamp

h2. Definition of “ground truth” for validation
We use *counterfactual approximations* and *observed before/after deltas* where possible:
1) *Natural experiments* (preferred): routes where configuration changed historically (e.g., caching enabled, batch params adjusted) with sufficient pre/post traffic.
2) *A/B or canary windows* (when available): explicit rollout periods with known change timestamps.
3) *Proxy replay* (fallback): simulate expected improvements using logged distributions and validated microbenchmarks for the same model/hardware class. (Used to bound error; not considered “observed truth”.)

We will label each validation example with a *truth tier* (T1/T2/T3) and report metrics by tier.

h1. Data sources and eligibility
h2. Telemetry sources
* Request aggregates per route/model/region:
  * QPS, concurrency distribution
  * Input/output token counts (p50/p95/p99)
  * Sequence length histograms
  * Latency distributions (p50/p95/p99)
  * Error rate (5xx/429/timeouts)
* Cache metrics (when enabled):
  * Cache hit rate, prefix match rate, eviction rate
  * Cache read/write latency (if instrumented)
* Cost attribution:
  * Per-route cost estimate ($) and/or GPU time proxy, aligned to billing window

h2. Validation window
* Default historical window: last 28 days
* Minimum traffic for

(if instrumented)
* Cost attribution:
  * Per-route cost estimate ($) and/or GPU time proxy, aligned to billing window

h2. Validation window
* Default historical window: last 28 days
* Minimum traffic for inclusion:
  * ≥ 50k requests in the baseline window *and*
  * ≥ 7 distinct days with traffic (to avoid one-off spikes)
* Minimum stability:
  * Baseline p95 latency coefficient of variation (CV) < 0.35 (unless explicitly investigating unstable routes)

h2. Exclusions
* Routes with known incident periods in the baseline or post-change window (unless the change itself is part of incident mitigation)
* Routes with major model version changes confounded with the optimization change (unless we can isolate via pinned model ID)

h1. Sampling strategy
We will build a validation set that is representative and stress-tests edge cases.

h2. Sampling frame
All orgs/projects enrolled in dogfood + selected beta candidates with adequate telemetry maturity.

We stratify by:
* Deployment mode: Hosted / Dedicated / Private (if telemetry is available)
* Model family: Llama-class vs Mistral-class vs other curated open models
* Route type: chat/generate vs embeddings (embeddings generally excluded for batching/caching suggestions beta)
* Region
* Traffic level: high (top 20%), mid (middle 60%), low (bottom 20% but meeting minimum traffic)
* Latency sensitivity: inferred from configured SLO tier (if available) or baseline p95

h2. Sample sizes (targets)
* T1 (natural experiment pre/post): 60 route-model pairs
* T2 (explicit rollout/A-B): 20 route-model pairs
* T3 (proxy replay only): 40 route-model pairs (used for bounding and regression testing)

Total target: 120 validation examples.

h2. Over-sampling known risky areas
We will intentionally include:
* Routes with high variance in input token length
* Routes with spiky concurrency
* Routes with high tail-latency sensitivity (baseline p95 > 2.5× p50)

h1. Methodology
h2. Pre/post analysis (T1/T2)
For each example, define:
* Baseline window: 7 days ending 24h before change
* Post window: 7 days starting 24h after change
(We add the 24h buffer to reduce effects of partial rollouts and cache warm-up.)

Compute observed deltas:
* Cost delta:
  * Δ$/request and Δ$/day (normalized by request volume)
* Latency delta:
  * Δp50, Δp95 (ms)
* Secondary checks:
  * Error rate change (timeouts/5xx), rate limiting events (429)

h2. Matching / confound control
To reduce bias from traffic drift:
* Match baseline and post periods by day-of-week and hour-of-day where possible.
* Reweight by input/output token distributions:
  * If post window has materially different token mix (JS divergence > 0.10), label as “token-shift confounded” and report separately.
* Exclude windows overlapping platform incidents or major capacity changes.

h2. Proxy replay (T3)
Use telemetry distributions (tokens, concurrency) and a hardware/model performance profile to predict:
* Expected throughput change
* Expected latency shift under batching/caching

h2. Proxy replay (T3)
Use telemetry distributions (tokens, concurrency) and a hardware/model performance profile to predict:

T3 is used to:

* Provide conservative bounds when no pre/post truth exists

h1. Error metrics and reporting
We report metrics at two levels: *per-suggestion* and *portfolio* (top-N suggestions).

h2. Primary error metrics (cost)
For each example i:
* Absolute error (AE): |ŝ_i − s_i|
* Relative error (RE): (ŝ_i − s_i) / max(|s_i|, ε)
  * Use ε = $10/day equivalent to avoid divide-by-near-zero blowups
* Weighted MAPE (wMAPE): Σ|ŝ_i − s_i| / Σ|s_i|
* Bias: mean(ŝ_i − s_i)

Where:
* ŝ_i = estimated savings ($/day)
* s_i = observed savings ($/day) from pre/post normalization

h2. Primary error metrics (latency)
* MAE for Δp50 and Δp95 (ms)
* Tail safety rate:
  * % examples where estimator predicts Δp95 ≤ +X ms but observed Δp95 > +X ms
  * We evaluate X ∈ {25ms, 50ms, 100ms} depending on latency tier

h2. Calibration / confidence evaluation
If estimator emits confidence bands or a confidence score:
* Coverage:
  * % of examples where observed savings falls within predicted [low, high] interval
* Monotonicity:
  * Higher confidence buckets should have lower wMAPE

h2. “Top opportunities” usefulness metric
Since the Console surfaces top opportunities, we evaluate ranking quality:
* Precision@K (K=5,10): fraction of top-K estimated savings suggestions that are also top-K observed savings (within tier)
* NDCG@K for ranking alignment

h2. Reporting slices
We will publish metrics by:
* Suggestion type: batching vs caching
* Truth tier: T1/T2/T3
* Traffic level and variance
* Model family and region

h1. Acceptance thresholds (beta)
These thresholds gate *beta expansion* (not dogfood experimentation).

h2. Cost estimation thresholds
For T1/T2 combined:
* wMAPE (savings $/day):
  * ≤ 35% overall
  * ≤ 45% in each major slice (batching/caching)
* Bias (mean ŝ − s):
  * ≤ +10% of mean observed savings (we prefer slight underestimation; any consistent overestimation must be investigated)
* Overestimation guardrail:
  * P(ŝ > 1.5× s) ≤ 20% for examples with s ≥ $50/day

h2. Latency impact thresholds
For T1/T2 combined:
* MAE(Δp95): ≤ 40ms overall
* Tail safety:
  * For routes labeled Low risk, observed Δp95 > +50ms should occur in ≤ 5% of examples
  * For Medium risk, observed Δp95 > +100ms should occur in ≤ 10% of examples

h2. Confidence and interval quality
If intervals are shown in-product for beta:
* 80% predicted intervals should have ≥ 75% empirical coverage (we accept slight under-coverage in beta but must track)
* Confidence buckets must be monotonic: highest-confidence bucket wMAPE ≤ lowest-confidence bucket wMAPE −

h2. Console safety requirements (non-metric)
* For any suggestion where telemetry coverage is insufficient (e.g., < 7 days or missing cache signals), the UI must:

h1. Execution plan
h2. Deliverables
1) Validation dataset manifest
* List of route/model/org identifiers (pseudonymized), truth tier, change timestamps, eligibility flags.
2) Reproducible evaluation notebook/pipeline
* Produces metric tables and slice dashboards.
3) Findings report
* Summary, key failure modes, recommended estimator adjustments and UI guardrails.

h2. Timeline
* Week 1: Build candidate list and truth-tier labeling; align with telemetry owners on availability.
* Week 2: Run T1/T2 evaluation; compute metrics and slices; identify systemic overestimation.
* Week 3: Patch estimator and re-run; finalize beta acceptance recommendation.

h1. Known failure modes to watch
* Token-shift confounding: post window has different prompt mix.
* Cache warm-up effects: early post window may understate benefits (or overstate if warmed by prior traffic).
* Hidden throttling: concurrency caps or rate-limits change between windows.
* Multi-change confounds: model version, kernel/runtime upgrade, or region capacity change coincident with config change.

Mitigations:
* Buffer windows around changes
* Label and report confounded examples rather than hiding them
* Conservative UI messaging when variance is high

h1. Documentation and customer-facing implications
* If we fail acceptance thresholds:
  * Do not expand beta cohort.
  * Tighten guardrails (suppress low-confidence suggestions) and adjust copy to emphasize uncertainty.

Slice Prioritization and Annotation Bidding Playbook

Summary

This playbook describes a reproducible, cross-signal method for prioritizing prompt slices for annotation and evaluation when annotation budget is constrained. It introduces an annotation-bidding mechanism that allocates labeling budget to slices based on combined signals from production telemetry, eval harness deltas, quantization sensitivity, and historical regression triage. The goal is to surface high-impact slices for human review quickly while minimizing cost and time-to-action.

Goals

- Reduce mean time to detection and remediation for priority quality regressions by 30% for high-volume slices.
- Allocate annotation budget to slices with the highest expected utility (quality delta * traffic exposure / annotation cost).
- Integrate seamlessly with eval-harness, model-onboarding checks, quant profiles, and regression triage workflows.

Scope

- Applies to prompt slices derived from production telemetry, synthetic probe farms, and onboarding probe sets.
- Covers prioritization, auction/bid configuration, annotation assignment, and downstream integration with triage and rollout.
- Excludes detailed annotator instructions (see annotation-stewardship page) and labeling UI implementation details.

Definitions

- Slice: A traffic or probe partition defined by intent, API route, user cohort, template family, or other attributes.
- Signal: Any numeric input for prioritization (e.g., traffic volume, delta score, quant-sensitivity).
- Bid: A computed, unitless priority score used to order slices for annotation allocation.

Signals and Weighting

We combine multiple orthogonal signals into a single bid score. Signals below are normalized to [0,1] before aggregation.

- Traffic exposure (W_traffic): 7-day average request count for slice normalized by max slice volume.
- Delta severity (W_delta): Change in eval-harness failure rate or quality metric vs baseline (example: -ROUGE or increased hallucination rate).
- Regression recurrence (W_recurrence): Count of prior regressions or triage incidents involving the slice in the past 90 days, scaled to [0,1].
- Quant-sensitivity (W_quant): Sensitivity score from quantization profile tests (probing same prompt family at target quant levels).
- Cost-per-annotation inverse (W_cost): 1 - (estimated annotation cost / max expected cost) to favor cheaper high-impact slices.

Scoring formula (example)

Bid = alpha*T + beta*D + gamma*R + delta*Q + epsilon*C

Where T,D,R,Q,C are the normalized signals and alpha..epsilon are weights. Default weights: alpha=0.30, beta=0.30, gamma=0.15, delta=0.15, epsilon=0.10. We recommend tuning weights per product line.

Procedure: End-to-end prioritization and annotation allocation

1. Ingest slices into the prioritization service. Inputs: slice id, 7-day traffic, eval-harness delta metrics, quant-sensitivity vector, last 90d regression events, annotation-cost estimates.
2. Normalize signals and compute Bid per slice using the scoring formula.
3. Produce a ranked queue of slices and assign annotation budget in bidding rounds (see auction below).
4. Create annotation tasks in the annotation system with metadata: slice_id, priority (bid), schema, target labels, and TTL.
5. After annotation completes, results are fed into eval-harness and

5. After annotation completes, results are fed into eval-harness and triage pipelines automatically: quality checks, delta re-computation, and regression alarm generation.
6. If annotations indicate a high-severity regression (see thresholds), trigger an immediate rollback or model fallback policy per regression triage runbook.

Auction / Bidding mechanism (budget-constrained rounds)

- Bidding rounds are 24-hour windows. Each round has a fixed annotation budget (tokens or USD) assigned by product/owner team.
- Slices bid based on computed Bid score; budget is allocated top-down until budget exhausted.
- Reserve up to 10% of budget each round for emergent slices flagged by SRE or urgent customer tickets.

Example allocation algorithm (pseudocode)

1. Sort slices by Bid desc.
2. For slice in sorted list:
   a. If slice.estimated_cost <= remaining_budget: assign full annotation block for slice.
   b. Else if remaining_budget > minimum_block: assign fractional sample proportional to remaining_budget and stop.

Annotation task definitions and sampling

- Block size: default 200 examples per full block (tunable by slice type).
- Minimum block: 25 examples (for exploratory sampling).
- Sampling strategy: stratified by route/intent and time-of-day to capture production variance.

Config table: prioritization service parameters

| Parameter | Description | Example default |
|---|---:|---:|
| weights | Comma-separated weights for T,D,R,Q,C | 0.30,0.30,0.15,0.15,0.10 |
| round_length_hours | Auction/bidding round length | 24 |
| default_block_size | Full annotation block size | 200 |
| min_block_size | Minimum exploratory block | 25 |
| reserve_budget_pct | Budget reserved for emergent slices | 10 |
| sensitivity_threshold | Quant-sensitivity threshold to mark "sensitive" | 0.6 |

CLI / API examples

- Compute bids for all active slices (example):
  $ rictl prioritize --space applied-ml --since 7d --weights 0.3,0.3,0.15,0.15,0.1 --out bids.csv

- Allocate annotation budget for a round:
  $ rictl allocate-annotation --round 2026-02-10 --budget-usd 2500 --reserve 10

- Export top N slices for annotation:
  $ rictl export-top --n 25 --format json --out /tmp/top25.json

Integration points and downstream actions

- Eval-harness: annotated labels are automatically ingested into the eval-harness dataset registry. New evaluations are scheduled using the same seed sets and metrics as the original reporting.
- Model-onboarding: onboarding runs include a prioritization pre-check so newly onboarded models immediately surface slices with high quant-sensitivity or coverage gaps.
- Regression triage: when annotated deltas exceed the triage severity threshold, the regression runbook is triggered and a triage ticket is created with links to annotated evidence and scalar plots.
- Observability: per-slice dashboards expose traffic, bid evolution, annotation status, and post-annotation delta.

Monitoring and SLOs

- Annotation turnaround SLO: 48 hours for full block annotations on high-priority slices (bid in top 10%).

- Annotation turnaround SLO: 48 hours for full block annotations on high-priority slices (bid in top 10%).
- Detection SLO: 95% of slices that cross the triage severity threshold should be annotated within two bidding rounds.
- Budget adherence: allocate <= 5% variance vs planned monthly annotation USD budget.

Decision thresholds and escalation rules

- Triage severity threshold: post-annotation delta >= 5% absolute regression in the primary quality metric (or a configurable alternative).
- Hot-slice escalation: if a slice shows >3 separate increments in delta across three successive rounds, escalate to oncall-evals for manual investigation.

Ownership and responsibilities

- Prioritization service owner: applied-ml platform team (pager: #applied-ml-prio).
- Annotation ops: data platform / annotation stewardship.
- Eval-harness integration: eval-platform team.
- Regression triage automation: model-reliability team.

Rollout plan

1. Pilot (2 weeks): run with 5 product slices, manual annotation handoff. Verify scoring signal alignment and label quality.
2. Beta (6 weeks): expand to 25 slices across two product lines; enable automated annotation task creation.
3. GA: enable full auction rounds, integrate reg triage triggers, and publish dashboards.

Rollback criteria

- Stop automated allocations if annotation quality (inter-annotator agreement) falls below 0.7 for two consecutive rounds.
- Revert to manual prioritization if the prioritization score shows instability (top-10 composition churn > 40% between rounds) for three rounds.

Frequently asked questions

Q: How are annotation-cost estimates derived?
A: Cost estimates are historical-cost-based per-label type and slice complexity heuristics (token counts, multi-turn context). They are recalibrated monthly.

Q: Can product teams override bids?
A: Yes — product owners can flag slices as "owner-priority" which adds a fixed boost (default +0.2) to the bid for a configurable number of rounds. Overrides are audited.

Service-aligned Probe Manifest and Priming Registry

This document defines a canonical, service-oriented probe manifest and a lightweight priming registry used to align evaluation probes with product services. It codifies fields, registration workflows, lifecycle rules, and the telemetry contract required to run production-representative evals across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
Background: As Redwood scales multi-tenant shadow and synthetic-probe evaluations, we need a single source-of-truth for probes that are explicitly mapped to product services and runtime characteristics. This registry ensures probes carry enough metadata for safe shadow execution (quant/kv-cache compatibility), prioritization, and reproducible priming used by evaluators and the runtime orchestration layer.

Goals:
- Map probes to logical service boundaries (service_id, route_pattern).
- Capture runtime compatibility (quant_profile, kv_cache_required, max_context_tokens).
- Store priming templates (few-shot examples / anchoring context) and their stability metadata.
- Provide a small-enough manifest to be embedded alongside probes in eval pipelines and retained in the eval asset registry.

Non-goals: This is not a replacement for the full probe asset registry or human-facing annotation logs. The manifest is intentionally compact and machine-oriented.
The manifest is a compact record attached to each probe. Fields (required/optional):
- probe_id (required): stable opaque id (rpid-xxxx).
- display_name (required): short human name.
- service_id (required): canonical product service (e.g., rerank-service-v2).
- route_pattern (optional): API route or logical route (e.g., /chat/*).
- workload_class (required): one of {interactive, batch, rerank, embedding}.
- quant_profile (optional): recommended quant profile id (e.g., q8h-coarse) or null.
- kv_cache_required (optional): boolean; true if probe expects long context cache behavior.
- max_context_tokens (optional): integer; used for routing and cost estimation.
- priming_template_id (optional): if priming present, pointer to priming registry entry.
- expected_stability_score (optional): float 0..1 used by CI gating.
- sampling_weight (optional): numeric weight used by scheduler.
- owner (required): team alias owning the probe (e.g., platform-evals).
- retention_policy (optional): short code: P90 (90d), P365 (365d), PRUNE (manual).
- tags (optional): list of short tags (strings).

Table: Example manifest fields and acceptable values are described inline above. Implementations must validate required fields before registration.
Registration workflow (1–2 engineers):
1) Author creates probe asset and a companion manifest JSON using the schema above. Use rpid-<sha1(artifact)> convention for probe_id.
2) Push manifest+probe to the eval-asset-store and request priming-template creation if required.
3) CI checks run: manifest validation, light syntactic eval (sanity response), tokenization check (max_context_tokens), and compatibility test against quant_profile if present.
4) Reviewer from owner team (owner) approves in the registry UI. Reviewer sign-off requires: owner approval and a passing sanity eval.
5) After approval the probe enters STAGED state and is available for shadow scheduling.
6) To promote to PROD probes must pass a 24h stochastic-stability window measured against service-specific slice anchors.

Notes: For probes that require customer-sensitive data,

STAGED state and is available for shadow scheduling.
6) To promote to PROD probes must pass a 24h stochastic-stability window measured against service-specific slice anchors.

Notes: For probes that require customer-sensitive data, mark confidentiality=restricted and attach a brief data-handling note in related_pages. Probes failing CI must include failure_reason and remediations in the registry UI.
Lifecycle states and TTLs:
- DRAFT: Not scheduled, editable by author. TTL: indefinite until submitted.
- STAGED: Visible to eval scheduler for shadow runs. Required: manifest validation, owner approval. TTL: 30d by default, auto-notify owner at T+21d.
- PROD: Rotational priority for long-term monitoring. Entry to PROD requires 24h stability pass and registration of telemetry anchors. Retention: P365 by default.
- DEPRECATED: Marked by owner; scheduler excludes by default but can be used for ad-hoc investigation.
- PRUNED: Removed from active registry; archived blob retained per retention_policy.

Lifecycle operations: update->retest->promote or update->fail->revert. Every state change must be recorded with a changelog entry including actor, timestamp, and reason.
All probes must emit or be accompanied by evaluation telemetry for the scheduler and RCA tooling. Required telemetry fields (names used in metrics/telemetry pipelines):
- eval.probe_id (string)
- eval.service_id (string)
- eval.run_id (string)
- eval.latency_p50_ms (number)
- eval.latency_p95_ms (number)
- eval.token_cost (number)
- eval.stability_score (number 0..1)  // composite metric comparing anchor outputs
- eval.confidence (optional float)
- eval.priming_version (string)
- eval.quant_profile_used (string)
- eval.kv_cache_hit_ratio (optional float)

SLOs and gating thresholds (defaults; service teams may set stricter values):
- Stability pass threshold: stability_score >= 0.92 over 1,000 probes in 24h window.
- Latency tail: p95 <= service latency_slo_p95_ms (service-specific; request in service manifest).
- Token-cost delta: median token_cost relative to baseline <= +15%.

Failure modes: Telemetry missing required fields -> auto-fail CI. Stability_score drop below 0.85 triggers immediate DEPRECATE flag and creates a regression triage ticket in #eval-regressions.

Instrumentation notes: Prefer the evaluator-sidecar to emit eval.* metrics; fallback is post-run ingestion using eval metadata. All telemetry must be taggable by region, deployment_type (hosted|dedicated|private), and model_variant.
Canary & rollout policy (recommended):
1) Micro-canary: run probe at 1% of production shadow traffic for 6h. Check stability and latency metrics.
2) Staged increase: 1% -> 10% -> 25% -> 100% over a 72h window, with health checks at each step.
3) Canary pass criteria: stability_score >= configured_threshold, no P95 tail regression > 2x baseline, and no functional sentinel failures.

Rollback steps (if any step fails):
- Immediate halt of rollout and automatically demote to STAGED.
- Open a regression incident and kick off cross-team Triage (see regression-triage playbook).
- If failure is quant-related, trigger quant-fallback policy: route traffic to a verified compatibility profile and notify runtime-ops to pin KV cache behavior.

Automated rollback hooks: the scheduler must support automated rollbacks when

If failure is quant-related, trigger quant-fallback policy: route traffic to a verified compatibility profile and notify runtime-ops to pin KV cache behavior.

Automated rollback hooks: the scheduler must support automated rollbacks when the aggregated severity score exceeds the configured rollback_threshold.
Owners and channels:
- Probe owner (manifest.owner): primary responsible for correctness and remediations.
- Evaluation steward (platform-evals): schedules weekly probe hygiene sweeps.
- Oncall: eval-oncall rotates; use pager duty (PD: eval-oncall) for high-severity regressions.
- Slack channels: #eval-ops (ops/questions), #eval-regressions (incidents), #probe-registry (onboarding questions).

Escalation matrix:
- Triage (severity low): owner @48h.
- Action (severity medium): owner + steward @8h.
- Incident (severity high): owner + steward + runtime-sre + product @1h and PD alert.

Priming templates must record version and a short changelog. The priming registry entry is small (max 8KB) and is stored alongside the probe manifest in the eval-asset-store.
Implementation notes for the runtime team:
- Scheduler must fetch manifest fields before selecting quant_profile and routing.
- If kv_cache_required=true and the runtime does not support long-context caching for the model_variant, mark the probe as INCOMPATIBLE and notify owner.
- Implement a small compatibility test harness that runs the probe against a lightweight shadow runtime (1e-3 sample ratio) before scheduling at scale.

Migration notes:
- For existing probes without manifests, run an automated harvest job that attempts to infer service_id, workload_class, and max_context_tokens and open an onboarding ticket for manual validation.

Glossary:
- Priming: few-shot or anchor context injected with a probe for behavioral anchoring.
- Stability_score: composite similarity metric used across anchors to detect semantic drift.
- Probe: a synthetic input + expected anchoring used for automated evals.

Annotator Economics and Probe Retention Policy

Summary:

This document defines Redwood Inference's policy for annotation economics (how we compensate human annotators and run quality control) and the lifecycle and retention policy for probe artifacts used across evals, model onboarding, and regression triage. The goal is to make probe stewardship predictable, cost-aware, privacy-compliant, and operationally auditable.

Scope:
- Applies to all probe artifacts generated or ingested by Applied ML and Evals teams, including synthetic probes, user-derived probes (anonymized), adversarial test cases, and annotator labels stored in central probe repositories.
- Includes guidance for annotator pay bands, QA pass thresholds, annotation latency targets, storage tiers, deletion/archival procedures, and exception handling.
- Excludes ephemeral debug probes created only in local development that are not pushed to shared repositories.

Definitions:
- Probe: an input (prompt, conversation, multimodal input) together with metadata and (optionally) reference labels used for evaluation.
- Annotator: a human contributor who provides labels, ratings, or quality judgments for probes. Includes internal annotators and vetted external vendors.
- Probe Artifact: files and records (JSON/YAML/CSV and attachments) stored in the probe catalog.
- Hot Storage: fast-access storage used by eval harnesses and live shadowing.
- Cold Storage: lower-cost blob storage (S3 Glacier/nearline) for archival.

Roles & Responsibilities:
- Applied ML (Probe Stewards): maintain probe taxonomy, label schema, and retention metadata fields. Primary owner of this policy.
- Data Platform: implements storage lifecycle rules, access controls, and cost reports.
- Vendor Management: negotiates vendor rates, SLAs, and compliance attestations.
- Security & Privacy: approves retention periods for customer-derived probes and redaction procedures.

Annotator economics (recommended bands and pay model):
- Payment model: per-labeled-item with QA-tier multiplier. Final payout = base_rate * (1 + qa_bonus) where qa_bonus depends on audit pass rate.
- Base rate bands (USD per judgment, approximate ranges):
  * Simple binary label: $0.06 - $0.12
  * Multi-class single-turn: $0.20 - $0.45
  * Multi-turn dialog (per-turn): $0.40 - $1.10
  * Complex reasoning / chain-of-thought annotation: $1.50 - $4.00
- QA multiplier: 
  * Audit pass >= 98%: +12% bonus
  * 95% <= pass < 98%: +6% bonus
  * 90% <= pass < 95%: +0% bonus
  * pass < 90%: action: retraining and partial rework; pay withheld until rework passes.
- Minimum effective hourly guarantee for internal annotators: $18/hr equivalent (useful for long tasks with many micro judgments).
- Vendor SLA expectations: average label latency < 48 hours for standard tasks, < 24 hours for high-priority probes. Penalties apply for repeated misses.

Quality control and instrumentation:
1) Sentinel audits: 5–10% of items randomly selected for gold checks per batch.
2) Inter-annotator agreement (IAA): report Cohen's Kappa or Krippendorff alpha per task; threshold: Kappa >= 0.65 for promotion to production probes.
3) Review pipeline:

3) Review pipeline: failed sentinels trigger reviewer queue; repeated failures escalate to vendor management.
4) Annotator feedback loop: weekly calibration sessions and example-led remediation.

Probe metadata and minimum schema (fields required in probe catalog):
- probe_id (string), created_by (string), created_at (YYYY-MM-DD), source (synthetic | shadow | customer), sensitivity_level (public | internal | restricted), retention_tier (hot | cold | delete_on_criteria), labels (list), annotator_id (string|vendor-id), qa_pass (true|false), qa_notes (string), last_accessed (YYYY-MM-DD), linked_eval_id (string), embargo_until (YYYY-MM-DD|null).

Retention policy (default tiers and TTLs):
- Hot (default for newly created probes): 180 days from created_at unless promoted. Accessible to eval harness and shadowing pipelines.
- Cold: 3 years from created_at. Moved to cold after 180 days of inactivity or explicit archival. Retrieval windows: 24–72 hours.
- Delete-on-criteria: immediate deletion after fulfillment of legal/contractual erasure requests or on-demand for restricted customer data after NDA review.
- Permanent archive: select seed sets (curated benchmarks) may be retained indefinitely; these must have explicit product owner approval and an associated retention waiver.

Data access and privacy controls:
- All customer-derived probes default to sensitivity_level=restricted unless redacted and approved by Privacy.
- Annotator access: annotators should not see raw PII. Use programmatic redaction and privacy-preserving interfaces.
- Access logs: every read/write/restore from cold storage must be logged with user, action, and timestamp. Audit log retention: 2 years.

Cost estimation and example table (monthly cost model):

Operational runbook: enforcement and typical procedures
1) Daily job: retention-enforcer runs at 02:00 UTC. Steps:
   a) Query probe_catalog for items where retention_tier=hot AND created_at < now() - 180d AND last_accessed < now() - 90d.
   b) For candidates, create a move-to-cold task and notify probe steward slack channel (#probe-stewards).
   c) When moving to cold, update retention_tier and set last_moved_to_cold timestamp.
2) Weekly audit: run a probe-ttl-audit report listing items scheduled for deletion within

task and notify probe steward slack channel (#probe-stewards).
   c) When moving to cold, update retention_tier and set last_moved_to_cold timestamp.
2) Weekly audit: run a probe-ttl-audit report listing items scheduled for deletion within 30 days. Notify owners.
3) Deletion procedure (manual gating for restricted):
   1. Verify legal/customer erasure token.
   2. Run redact-and-delete CLI (example below).
   3. Append deletion event to retention_audit_log.

Metrics and dashboards (what to monitor):
- Annotation throughput (labels/day) by vendor and task type. Target: sustained throughput with <15% variance week-over-week.
- QA pass rate (gold sentinel pass %) per batch. SLO: >= 95%.
- Average time-to-label (mean and p95). Target: mean < 24h for standard tasks.
- Probe catalog storage by tier (GB) and monthly cost. Budget variance alert: >10% increase month-over-month triggers finance review.
- Retention compliance rate: % of probes older than TTL that are still in hot storage (target < 1%).

Onboarding and pay adjustment flow for new tasks:
1) Probe steward drafts task spec and rough complexity estimate.
2) Run pilot with 500 items and measure median time-per-item and QA pass rate.
3) Compute effective hourly equivalent and map to base_rate band.
4) Submit vendor rate change request with evidence (pilot metrics).
5) After 2 successful pilot batches (consistent IAA and QA), promote task to production pricing.

Exception handling and retention waivers:
- Retention waivers must be recorded as a short-form ADR in Applied ML with owner signoff and expiration date.
- Emergency retention freeze (e.g., ongoing incident triage): applied-ml-oncall may freeze deletion for up to 30 days; approval and rationale logged.

Audit and compliance:
- Monthly compliance digest emailed to Security & Privacy and Finance summarizing retention transitions, deletions, vendor spend, and active waivers.
- Random third-party audit: once per year, a vendor (approved by Legal) may audit probe handling.

Workload Edge-Case Habitat and Probe Synthesis Cookbook

Overview:
This cookbook defines a repeatable, low-friction process for discovering, synthesizing, and stewarding probe artifacts that exercise the long tail and brittle edge cases in production LLM workloads. It bridges prompt set generation, eval-harness ingestion, model-onboarding acceptance criteria, quantization sensitivity checks, and regression triage handoffs.

Why this exists:
- Edge-case failures are low-frequency but high-impact for user experience and downstream regressions.
- Synthesized probes enable safe, private, and repeatable stress-testing without exposing customer data.
- A single source-of-truth for probe format and telemetry makes downstream tooling (evaluators, alerting, rollback) deterministic.

Scope:
- Applies to: interactive chat, reranking, few-shot instruction-following, functioncall-heavy flows.
- Not covered: image-only or strictly offline batch embedding workloads (see separate multimodal playbooks).

Definitions:
- Probe: a single input + metadata + expected-signal set designed to exercise a behavior slice.
- Habitat: the contextual envelope (user persona, system prompt, long context, latency constraints) in which a probe is valid.
- Synthesizer: the process (automated or human-in-loop) that generates probes from seeds.
- Probe Manifest: canonical table of probes, ownership, and lifecycle state.

High-level workflow (summary):
1) Threat model & slice definition (owner: product/ML writer)
2) Seed collection (real traffic + adversarial templates)
3) Synthesis pass (automated paraphrase, noise injection, context morphing)
4) Filtering & tagging (sanitization, privacy gating)
5) Telemetry annotation and ingestion contract creation
6) Eval-harness ingestion and tiered prioritization
7) Onboarding acceptance checks (quant, latency, coherence)
8) Regression triage hooks and escalation mapping

Detailed steps: 
1) Threat model & slice definition
- Output: 1-page slice brief with a hypothesis, impact statement, and acceptance SLI. Example SLI: "semantic-preservation@95p >= 0.92 on 1k probes".
- Required fields: owner, use-case, primary model family affected, example failure modes.

2) Seed collection
- Inputs: anonymized production examples (if available), customer-reported tickets, synthetic adversarial templates from security team.
- Minimum seed size: 200 unique examples per high-priority slice, 50 for exploratory slices.

3) Synthesis pass (automated stages)
- Paraphrase generation: beam paraphrase with edit-distance threshold > 6 tokens.
- Noise injection: punctuation removal, repeated tokens, unicode confusables, code-switching (probability 0.12).
- Context morphing: move relevant history earlier/later; insert benign distractor turns.
- For functioncall services: vary function argument order, type coercion ("42" vs 42), and missing optional keys.
- Output: candidate probes with provenance tags (synth_tool:v1, seed_id).

4) Filtering & tagging
- Privacy filter rules: drop any candidate with > 0.45 probability of containing PII according to pii-detector:v2.
- Tagging taxonomy (example): slice:payment-confusion, intent:refund, modality:text-only, severity:critical|major|minor.

5) Telemetry annotation and ingestion contract
- Telemetry fields (required): probe_id, slice, seed_provenance, synth_tool_version, expected_signal_labels, created_by, creation_ts.
- Runtime capture to request log: probe_id, request_qualifier (shadow/canary/live), model_variant, latency_ms, token_count_input, token_count_output, response_signature_hash, kv-cache-hit(bool), quant-path(label).
- Ingestion frequency: batched

6) Eval-harness ingestion and prioritization
- Priority buckets: P0 (customer-facing regression risk), P1 (quality drift observable), P2 (research/coverage).
- Scheduling heuristic (textual): allocate at least 5% of continuous eval budget to rotating P0 probes; maintain a hot-set of 500 P0 probes per model family.

7) Onboarding acceptance checks (sample checklist)
- Coherence: semantic similarity score delta < 0.06 against golden responses on deterministic seed set.
- Functioncall fidelity: 100% structured-output parseability on 200 probes.
- Quant safety: no more than 1.5% of probes show coherence failures attributable to quant path (per quant-profile).
- Latency: 95th percentile latency on target infra < SLO threshold for this slice.
- If any check fails, route to "probe-failure-review" with triage notes.

8) Regression triage hooks and escalation mapping
- Every failing probe must create a triage ticket with: failing-model-variant, observed-signal, golden-sample, recent-deploy-commit, telemetry snapshot link.
- Owner routing: if failure correlates with quant-profile tag -> quant-team; timestamped prefix cache anomalies -> serving-runtime; otherwise -> model-owner.
