Release Preflight and Change Classification for Inference

A prescriptive change-classification and preflight checklist for inference-related releases (API, model, infra, and observability). Establishes gates, ownership, test signals, and rollback criteria to minimize production regressions while enabling safe velocity.
Purpose
This document defines a standardized classification for changes that affect Redwood Inference serving (APIs, runtime kernels, model variants, routing policies, and infra) and a corresponding preflight checklist and gating rules. The goal is to reduce production regressions, shorten outage blast radius, and make rollout/rollback decisions predictable.

Scope
Applies to any change that will be deployed to: hosted inference control plane, serving runtime (kernels, scheduling), model catalog entries (version/quantization changes), routing policies (fallbacks, region routing), or API surface changes that can affect latency or correctness. It does not replace product design reviews for feature requirements.

Change classification
1) LEVEL 0 — Configuration tweak (low-risk)
- Examples: Logging verbosity, dashboard retention window, non-path impacting feature flags.
- Approval: Owner sign-off in PR; automated unit + lint tests.
- Deployment: Direct to main with standard CI; optional canary.

2) LEVEL 1 — Behavioral change (medium-risk)
- Examples: Default batching window change, autoscaling parameter tweak, telemetry sampling rate, non-breaking API header addition.
- Approval: Owner + infra/test reviewer.
- Tests: Integration tests, canary with synthetic traffic, perf smoke (99th latency and token cost).
- Deployment: Canary 5–10% for 24 hours; automated rollback on SLI degradation.

3) LEVEL 2 — Compatibility-impacting change (high-risk)
- Examples: Model parameter update (changes generation quality), API contract modification (schema optional->required), KV-cache semantics changes.
- Approval: Design review + product + SRE review.
- Tests: End-to-end evaluation against canonical prompt set, regression test suite, cost delta estimate, security review if data-path changes.
- Deployment: Progressive rollout (canary -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with manual gate at each step and a 48-hour observation window.

4) LEVEL 3 — Safety/Regulatory or P0 risk (critical)
- Examples: Data residency changes, encryption/KMS swaps, rollback of major routing fallback behavior, change that can silently leak PII.
- Approval: Exec-level sign-off, legal/security consult, cross-team incident readiness.
- Tests: Audit logs verification, privacy review, full DR rehearsal.
- Deployment: Restricted maintenance window, 2-person release, immediate rollback playbook prepared.

Preflight checklist (cross-cutting, required fields)
Owners must include a completed preflight report attached to the PR or release ticket. Minimum items: 
- Change classification (Level 0–3) and rationale.
- List of owners and on-call contacts (primary, backup).
- Affected services and endpoints (service names, k8s deployment names, model ids).
- API compatibility statement (breaking/non-breaking, client impact).
- Test matrix results: unit, integration, perf-smoke, evals (pass/fail + links).
- Telemetry and SLI baselines: 50th/95th/99th latency, error rate, tokens/sec cost estimate.
- Observability additions required: dashboards, alert thresholds, tracing hooks,

- Test matrix results: unit, integration, perf-smoke, evals (pass/fail + links).
- Telemetry and SLI baselines: 50th/95th/99th latency, error rate, tokens/sec cost estimate.
- Observability additions required: dashboards, alert thresholds, tracing hooks, new metric names.
- Rollout plan: canary percentages, duration, automated/manual gates, rollback criteria.
- Backout steps and runbook link (must include commands and time estimate).
- Security and compliance impact assessment (PII, KMS, network).
- Feature-flag or routing config for rapid disable.

Automated gates and gating signals
The following signals must be wired into the deployment pipeline for Level 1+ changes: 
- Error rate anomaly: +3x baseline sustained during 5m window -> fail canary.
- Latency SLO breach: 99th percentile increases by >20% or absolute > target for 10m -> fail.
- Cost per token delta: >15% increase over expected at canary throughput -> alert and require sign-off.
- Quality regression (Level 2): automated evals on the canonical prompt set must not regress beyond configured thresholds (per-prompt ROUGE/embedding distance/LLM-quality metric).
- Trace sampling coverage: new endpoints must emit trace id and sampling rate >= 10% in canary.

Rollback criteria (minimal actionable conditions)
- Immediate rollback if: sustained error rate > 2x baseline for 10m, or customer-impacting 5xx spike affecting >1% of traffic, or manual escalations from on-call indicating severe functional regression.
- Conditional rollback: increase in latency SLO violations > threshold for 30m without remediation.
- Quality-triggered rollback: regression tests show meaningful decline on >5% of core prompt set, or automated user-sentiment signal crosses configured threshold.

Runbook snippets (examples)
- Quick rollback (hosted API routing revert):
  1) curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" https://console.redwood/api/v1/routing/revert -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","to":"stable"}'
  2) kubectl -n serving rollout undo deployment/serve-runtime --to-revision=<prev>
  3) run scripts/observability/check-rollout-health.sh --window 15m

- Drain-and-validate (stateful kernel change):
  1) Mark node pool as cordon: kubectl cordon <node>
  2) Start controlled drains and observe KV cache miss rate: metrics "serve.kv_cache_miss_rate"
  3) If miss rate > 10% for > 5m, abort and rollback.

Observability and dashboards
Required dashboards for any Level 1+ rollout:
- Per-route latency (p50/p95/p99), per-model token cost, error type breakdown (4xx/5xx), and request volume.
- Canary vs baseline comparison panel with percent-delta.
- Model-quality metric panels (automated eval pass rate, embedding drift heatmap).
- Incident trigger dashboard: rollup view showing anomalies across latency, errors, and customer SLOs.

SLO thresholds and cost guardrails (example table)
| Signal | Canary threshold | Production threshold | Action |
|--------|------------------|---------------------|--------|
| p99 latency | <= baseline * 1.2 | <= target | Fail canary / page SRE |
| Error rate (5xx) | <= baseline * 3 | <= baseline * 1.5 | Fail canary / alert |
| Tokens per request cost | <= +15% | <= +5% | Alert /

rate (5xx) | <= baseline * 3 | <= baseline * 1.5 | Fail canary / alert |
| Tokens per request cost | <= +15% | <= +5% | Alert / sign-off |
| Model eval pass rate | >= 98% | >= 99% | Fail if regression |

(Represented here in text; release-ticket templates include a machine-parsable YAML table.)

Testing and evaluation requirements
- Every Level 2 change must run the canonical evaluation harness (applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness) with a deterministic seed and include a short report with metrics, counterexamples, and suggested mitigations.
- Integration tests must exercise real batching shapes (max token sequences, heavy concurrency) rather than synthetic single-request patterns. CI must surface token-cost estimates for the change.

Ownership and roles
- Change owner: responsible for preflight, rollout, and rollback.
- Release coordinator: orchestrates canary schedule and manual gates.
- SRE: owns alerting thresholds and executes rollback on SLO breach.
- Product/ML owner: signs off on quality evals for model-impacting changes.

Enforcement and compliance
- PR checks: the code review CI will validate the presence of a completed preflight fields file (preflight.yaml) for Level 1+; absence blocks merge.
- Post-release audit: all Level 2+ changes will be subject to a 7-day postmortem-lite where telemetry and incident logs are reviewed.
- Exceptions: temporary exceptions must be documented and approved by SRE lead and the VP of Engineering.

Adoption guidance 
- Start with enforcement for Level 2 and Level 3 changes in Q1 2026. Level 1 enforcement (automated gating) should be phased in after we deploy the canary telemetry pipes (expected Jan 2026).
- Templates and CI jobs: a release-ticket template and a preflight.yaml schema are provided in the team wiki. Use the provided GitHub Action to post canary metrics to the release ticket.

Decision and rationale
We chose a classification-focused approach to balance developer velocity with safety. The key trade-offs considered:
- Conservative gating reduces incidents but increases lead time for risky changes. To mitigate this, we emphasize automated evaluation and parallelizable preflight tasks.
- Cost sensitivity: we include token-cost estimates in the preflight because model updates can silently double cost.
- Human-in-the-loop: manual gates remain for Level 2+ to capture nuanced quality judgments that automated metrics may miss.

adr-traffic-tagging-cost-allocation-2026

Summary:

This ADR documents the decision to adopt a fine-grained traffic tagging and telemetry enrichment model to support per-tenant cost allocation, cost-aware routing, and improved observability. The goal is to enable accurate billing attribution for multi-tenant workloads, provide signal for routing/capacity decisions, and preserve tenant privacy and performance.

Context and problem statement:

- Redwood runs mixed tenancy across Hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments. The cost of inference (GPU time, host CPU, memory, network egress) must be attributed to customers for billing and internal chargeback.
- Existing telemetry streams capture coarse route and model metrics but lack deterministic per-request cost attribution (e.g., token counts attributed to tenant + route + model variant).
- We need a solution that:
  - Correlates inference resource consumption to a tenant and request-level dimensions (model, sequence length, features used).
  - Enables real-time and nearline cost-allocation for billing accuracy within 0.5% on large accounts and explanatory granularity for small accounts.
  - Preserves tenant privacy (no sensitive prompt content in telemetry) and minimizes performance impact on latency-critical paths.
  - Supports both hosted and private deployments with consistent-enough schema for central processing.

Decision:

Adopt a two-layer approach: 1) deterministic request-level tagging in the inference control plane with a compact, non-sensitive enrichment payload, and 2) a downstream cost attribution pipeline that combines tagged telemetry with resource-metering from the runtime and GPU telemetry to produce final chargeable metrics.

Key aspects:

1) Request tagging contract (on-path, at ingress):

- Each incoming request must include or be stamped with a Traffic-Tag header (X-RW-Traffic-Tag) that encodes the canonical tenant id, route id, and a privacy-safe request-class hint.
- The header value format is a compact base64-encoded JSON Web Token (JWT) signed by Redwood's control plane key in hosted contexts. For private deployments, the local control plane issues signed tags using the customer's local key.
- Example (conceptual):

  X-RW-Traffic-Tag: eyJ0IjoiY2xpZW50OjEyMyIsInIiOiJzZXJ2aWNlX3RleHQiLCJwIjoiY29zdF9pZCJ9.SIGNATURE

- The decoded payload contains only non-sensitive identifiers and a request_class field chosen from a small enum: {interactive, batch, streaming, embed, internal}. No prompt or user text is included.

2) On-path lightweight telemetry enrichment (inference proxies and runtime):

- The serving proxy (ingress) appends a structured telemetry envelope to the request context that contains: tenant_id, route_id, model_variant, request_class, token_budget_hint, client_region, and correlation_id.
- This envelope is propagated with the request and emitted as a small structured log event at request start and request end. The end event must include final token counts: prompt_tokens, generated_tokens, total_tokens, and inference_latency_ms.
- Structured log example (pseudo-JSON event):

  {
    "event": "inference.request.end",
    "tenant_id": "tenant-123",
    "route_id": "route-abc",
    "model_variant": "redwood-v2-13b-q4",
    "request_class": "interactive",
    "prompt_tokens": 42,
    "generated_tokens": 128,
    "total_tokens": 170,
    "inference_latency_ms": 190,
    "gpu_ms": 120.5
  }

- IMPORTANT: No prompt or completions text are emitted. Any developer changes that introduce free-form text into telemetry must be gated by security review.

3) Runtime resource metering integration:

- GPU-time and per-container CPU/memory attribution

IMPORTANT: No prompt or completions text are emitted. Any developer changes that introduce free-form text into telemetry must be gated by security review.

3) Runtime resource metering integration:

- GPU-time and per-container CPU/memory attribution will be captured at the process/container level as periodic metrics (sampled at 1s). A deterministic per-request attribution uses token-based proportional allocation for shared processes when batches overlap requests.
- Kernel-level GPU metrics (SM utilization, GPU memory alloc) will be joined with request start/end times in the cost pipeline.

4) Cost-attribution pipeline (nearline):

- A nearline pipeline will consume request start/end events, resource meter streams, and batch scheduling logs to produce a cost record per request. This pipeline runs in the analytics cluster and creates final chargeable records exported to billing and cost dashboards.
- The pipeline must support backfills and reprocessing with idempotent joins using correlation_id.

5) Privacy and retention rules:

- Telemetry that contains tenant_id, route_id, and token counts is retained for 400 days for billing and audit. Raw per-request logs are redacted for PII and prompt text.
- Access to per-request telemetry is restricted to roles: billing-analyst, infra-observability, runtime-debug (requires approval). All access is audited.

6) Performance and safety constraints:

- On-path enrichment must add less than 0.3ms p95 latency at the ingress for interactive requests when properly optimized. Microbenchmarks should be executed in PRs that modify the traffic-tag stamping path.
- Telemetry serialization must be zero-copy where possible; use binary protobufs for RPC internal channels and structured JSON for log sinks.

7) Backwards compatibility and rollouts:

- Backwards compatibility: if a request lacks X-RW-Traffic-Tag, the ingress will synthesize a best-effort tag based on API key metadata and mark request_class=interactive and source=legacy. Synthesized tags include a synthetic flag for downstream filtering.
- Rollout plan: incremental gating by tenant cohort: internal-only -> 5% hosted traffic -> 25% -> 100% over 4 weeks, with canary on dedicated clusters. Private customers must opt into local tagging via the next private control-plane release; it will not be imposed automatically.

Alternatives considered (and why rejected):

- Piggybacking prompt-level content into telemetry for more precise usage breakdowns: rejected due to PII risk and retention compliance.
- Offline batch sampling and heuristics without request-level tags: rejected because it yields non-deterministic billing variance unacceptable for large accounts.
- Per-model resource metering only (no request tags): rejected because it can’t attribute costs across revisions, routes, and multi-model flows accurately.

Operational runbook (high level):

1) On alert: elevated billing drift (>1% vs expected) for top 10 tenants. Run the billing attribution re-run job with windowed reprocessing and compare pre/post.
2) On telemetry gaps: verify ingress tag stamping service health, check signing key rotation logs, and confirm message delivery to the analytics pipeline.
3) For privacy incidents: revoke downstream access and engage security + legal. Run a targeted re-redaction if necessary.

SLOs, constraints and metrics to track:

-

3) For privacy incidents: revoke downstream access and engage security + legal. Run a targeted re-redaction if necessary.

SLOs, constraints and metrics to track:

- Tag stamping success rate: 99.99% p30-day.
- Downstream cost record freshness: 95% records available in billing table within 10 minutes of request end.
- Attribution accuracy (sample validation): >=99.5% on large tenants (monthly audit).
- Telemetry ingestion error rate: <0.05% per day.

Implementation checklist and owners:

- Control plane: implement token signing + X-RW-Traffic-Tag issuance (owner: product-identity team).

- Approval board: eng-platform lead, finance lead, security lead.

ADR-015: Admission control layering for hosted overload protection (Gateway vs Routing vs Runtime)

## Status
Published (effective for Hosted API overload protection rollout).

## Context
Redwood Inference’s Hosted API sees bursty and highly variable traffic (prompt length variance, streaming concurrency spikes, regional capacity dips). During overload, failures can cascade into:
- Tail-latency blowups (p95/p99), then timeouts
- Elevated 5xx from upstream retry storms and downstream saturation
- Noisy-neighbor effects across tenants and tiers
- Confusing customer experience (timeouts and generic 5xx instead of stable semantics)

We need a layered admission control strategy that:
1) Rejects or degrades traffic early and predictably.
2) Preserves tenant isolation and tier-aware behavior.
3) Avoids feedback loops (e.g., shedding causing routing thrash, or routing failover amplifying load elsewhere).
4) Produces consistent customer-facing overload errors (see ADR-014).

This ADR defines **where circuit breakers and load shedding “live”** across the request path (Gateway → Routing → Runtime) and how signals flow.

## Decision
We will implement **layered admission control** with distinct responsibilities:

### 1) Gateway admission control (primary front-door protection)
**Gateway owns “who gets in”** based on:
- Tenant/tier policy (Hosted self-serve vs enterprise Hosted vs Dedicated routing paths)
- Per-route/model caps (concurrency, QPS/token-bucket style limits)
- Coarse-grained regional overload state (from aggregated signals)
- Dependency health gates for gateway-local dependencies (auth, quota/usage checks, policy engine, routing service)

Gateway behavior under overload:
- Return customer-facing errors per ADR-014 (typically 429 or 503 with stable overload error codes).
- Include correlation_id and consistent Retry-After semantics.
- Prefer **fail fast** when signals indicate sustained overload (avoid letting requests queue indefinitely).

Gateway does **not** attempt fine-grained GPU scheduling decisions.

### 2) Routing admission + fallback (secondary protection and graceful degradation)
**Routing owns “where it goes”** and **controlled degradation**, not global rate limiting.

Routing responsibilities:
- Choose region/model deployment target using policy (latency/cost/availability) and health signals.
- If gateway-admitted traffic hits a saturated target, routing may:
  - Attempt **configured fallback model/region** (bounded, loop-safe) when policy allows.
  - Otherwise, return an overload response consistent with ADR-014.

Routing must not create uncontrolled amplification (e.g., fan-out retries across regions). Routing is permitted to do **at most one** fallback attempt per request, and must enforce loop-prevention.

### 3) Runtime admission/backpressure (last-line protection)
**Runtime owns “what can actually execute”** on a given GPU pool/node.

Runtime responsibilities:
- Enforce hard safety limits: queue depth, scheduler backlog, token/sec saturation, memory/KV-cache pressure.
- Apply backpressure locally (e.g., refuse new admissions to a saturated scheduler; clamp optional features if configured).
- Export saturation signals at bounded cardinality for upstream decisions.

Runtime should be able to reject quickly with an internal reason that maps to stable overload error codes at the edge (ADR-014). Runtime should not attempt cross-region balancing.

### Summary: decision table
| Layer | Owns | Should do | Must not do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gateway | Early rejection + tenant/tier fairness | Token bucket / concurrency caps, dependency circuit breakers, consistent overload responses | GPU-level scheduling decisions, multi-step retry/fallback loops |
| Routing | Target selection + bounded graceful degradation | Single bounded fallback attempt (if configured), loop prevention, target health gating | Global rate limiting, unbounded retries, per-GPU fairness |
| Runtime | Local safety + scheduling viability | Backpressure, queue/kv/memory safety, feature clamping (policy-controlled), export saturation signals | Cross-region routing decisions, customer-specific policy interpretation |

## Rationale
### Why not “only gateway”?
Gateway-only decisions lack the most accurate, immediate view of per-pool saturation. If the gateway admits traffic without runtime backpressure, overload still manifests as long queues/timeouts. Runtime is the source of truth for “can this execute now?”.

### Why not “only runtime”?
Runtime-only rejection is too late:
- Wastes work in upstream services (auth, routing, logging, request parsing)
- Increases tail latency due to queue buildup
- Fails to enforce tenant/tier fairness consistently across services
Gateway is best suited to shed early and protect downstreams.

### Why involve routing?
Routing is the only layer that can safely implement **graceful degradation** (fallback model/region) and integrate capacity/health signals across targets. However, routing must be strictly bounded to avoid shifting overload around the system.

### Avoiding feedback loops
Layering introduces risks of control loops where:
- Gateway sheds → routing sees less traffic and declares healthy → gateway admits more → oscillation
- Runtime rejects → routing fails over → overload moves to another region → cascading rejection

We mitigate these via:
- **Hysteresis and smoothing** on saturation signals used by gateway and routing.
- **Single-step bounded fallback** (no multi-hop) and strict loop-prevention.
- **Separation of timescales** (runtime reacts fastest; gateway/routing react slower with stabilized aggregates).

## Signal flow (normative)
This section is normative for implementation.

### Runtime → telemetry → routing/gateway (aggregated)
Runtime exports saturation metrics at pool/cluster granularity:
- scheduler_queue_depth (gauge)
- scheduler_backlog_ms (gauge)
- token_throughput_utilization (0..1)
- kv_cache_pressure (0..1)
- memory_pressure_proxy (0..1)

A telemetry aggregation layer produces:
- per-region/per-model “saturation state” (e.g., normal / elevated / critical)
- smoothed utilization signals (EMA or rolling windows)
- recommended admission modifiers (e.g., suggested shed percent)

Gateway and routing consume **aggregated** signals; they should not consume high-cardinality per-node metrics.

### Gateway → routing (request-scoped hints)
When gateway admits a request, it may attach request-scoped metadata:
- tenant_id, tier
- route/model requested
-

**aggregated** signals; they should not consume high-cardinality per-node metrics.

### Gateway → routing (request-scoped hints)
When gateway admits a request, it may attach request-scoped metadata:
- tenant_id, tier
- route/model requested
- admission priority class (derived from policy)
- idempotency key presence (if provided by client)

Gateway must not encode dynamic “try these three regions” plans; routing remains responsible for selection.

### Routing → gateway/runtime (bounded outcomes)
Routing returns one of:
- Success (target selected)
- Overload response (with stable overload code)
- Success after single fallback attempt (internally recorded)

Routing should not instruct gateway to immediately open/close breakers. Gateway breaker state changes must come from its own breaker logic using stabilized aggregates and its local dependency health.

## Circuit breaker placement
We define three breaker types:

1) **Gateway dependency breakers** (fast, local)
- Trips on: auth/usage service latency/timeouts, policy-engine unavailability, routing service brownout
- Action: fail closed with stable 503 (dependency_unavailable) or 429/503 overload class per ADR-014 mapping

2) **Gateway overload breakers** (regional, policy-driven)
- Trips on: sustained regional saturation state = critical AND shed budget exceeded OR error-budget protection triggers
- Action: shed by tier/tenant/route with predictable semantics; include Retry-After

3) **Runtime safety breakers** (hard stop)
- Trips on: queue depth hard limit, memory pressure beyond threshold, scheduler unable to admit
- Action: reject immediately; propagate internal reason for edge mapping

Routing uses “health gates” rather than circuit breakers for most target selection decisions. Routing may maintain a short-lived “avoid target” cache with hysteresis to reduce flapping.

## Policy and configuration boundaries
- Tier defaults (Hosted self-serve, enterprise Hosted, Dedicated) live in the overload policy engine and are enforced primarily at gateway.
- Per-tenant overrides are evaluated at gateway and must be validated with guardrails (e.g., cannot exceed global safety caps).
- Runtime receives only what it needs for execution and safety (e.g., max_tokens cap adjustments or feature flags), not tenant policy logic.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Earlier, clearer shedding reduces tail latency and incident severity.
- Tenant/tier fairness is enforced consistently at the edge.
- Runtime remains protected even if gateway/routing misestimate load.
- Routing provides graceful degradation (fallback) without turning into a retry storm engine.

### Negative / tradeoffs
- More moving parts: three layers must align on semantics and observability.
- Tuning is non-trivial; requires careful rollout with canaries and dashboards.
- Signal aggregation adds latency; gateway decisions may lag rapid runtime changes (mitigated by runtime hard limits).

## Operational guidance (brief)
- When overload happens, prefer adjusting gateway policy thresholds and shed behavior before touching runtime queue settings.
- Use routing fallback only for tenants that have explicitly opted in and where compatible models are defined.
- Watch for oscillation: frequent

thresholds and shed behavior before touching runtime queue settings.
- Use routing fallback only for tenants that have explicitly opted in and where compatible models are defined.
- Watch for oscillation: frequent breaker open/close events or high fallback attempt rates are indicators of unstable thresholds.

## Implementation notes (non-normative)
- Gateway admission should use a combination of:
  - token bucket (QPS) per tenant/route
  - concurrency caps for streaming endpoints
  - “regional overload state” multiplier for dynamic throttling (with hysteresis)
- Runtime should expose clear “reject reasons” that map into ADR-014 overload codes without leaking internals.
- Routing should mark fallback attempts and enforce max_attempts=1. Any further attempt must be a client retry honoring Retry-After.

## Alternatives considered
1) **Single global breaker at gateway only**
- Rejected: insufficient fidelity; cannot protect runtime safety in all cases; still allows deep queueing.

2) **Runtime-only backpressure (let everything in)**
- Rejected: overload manifests as queued latency/timeouts; poor customer semantics; wastes upstream work.

3) **Routing-driven global admission control**
- Rejected: routing is not the best place to enforce tenant fairness and local dependency breakers; risks complex control loops.

## Open questions / follow-ups
- Define standard hysteresis parameters for “regional saturation state” (window sizes, open/close thresholds) and document in the policy engine page.
- Confirm SLO accounting and error budget treatment for overload-induced errors (tracked in Hosted API SLO policy update).
- Validate that runtime exported signals remain bounded cardinality and are stable under rolling deploys.

ADR: Fairness model for shared burst pools (Dedicated Burst Capacity)

## Status
Published (approved for implementation).

## Summary
We need a fairness model for *shared, Redwood-managed burst pools* used by Dedicated customers to temporarily exceed baseline reserved GPU capacity.

This ADR compares fairness approaches (WFQ, token buckets, priority tiers) and selects an implementation that:
- Prevents noisy-neighbor outcomes and reduces tail latency amplification for non-burst workloads.
- Produces deterministic, supportable admission decisions (same input → same decision) even under telemetry lag.
- Is measurable: we can quantify whether the fairness model is working via explicit metrics and guardrails.

## Context
Dedicated Burst Capacity allows a tenant (customer) to request additional capacity beyond their reserved baseline by borrowing from a shared burst pool (scoped to a region + hardware class, e.g., us-east/H100).

Key constraints:
- Baseline Dedicated capacity is not shared; only the incremental *burst portion* is.
- Burst pools must protect:
  1) Other Dedicated tenants using the same pool (including other bursters)
  2) Platform-wide SLOs and fleet safety limits
- Admission must be quick (p50 < 5ms in-controller) and safe under degraded telemetry conditions.
- The system must provide clear denial reasons to customers and Support.

Non-goals for the initial implementation:
- Spot-market style bidding / trading reservations.
- Cross-region bursting.
- Fully preemptive scheduling on GPU nodes (we do not preempt running model server processes per request).

## Decision drivers
1) **Measurable fairness**: ability to compute “share of pool granted vs entitled” per tenant/tier over time.
2) **Determinism**: avoids flapping decisions that lead to retry storms and hard-to-explain outcomes.
3) **Simplicity & operability**: few knobs; predictable behavior; easy to simulate in load tests.
4) **Anti-starvation**: ensure that small burst requests are not perpetually denied by one large tenant.
5) **Tail-latency protection**: keep queue depth and saturation in check; degrade gracefully when pool is hot.

## Considered options
### Option A: Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ) / Deficit Round Robin (DRR) at admission time
**Description:** Maintain per-tenant queues (or virtual finish times) and admit according to WFQ/DRR weights.

**Pros**
- Strong fairness properties in networking contexts.
- Can provide explicit weighted shares.

**Cons / risks**
- Requires maintaining queue state per tenant and per pool at high cardinality.
- Admission decisions become dependent on controller-local ordering; determinism across replicas becomes difficult without a shared ordered log.
- Harder to reason about under retries and client-driven concurrency (admit order may diverge).
- We do not have a single central queue per pool; routing paths are distributed.

**Conclusion:** Not selected for v1.

### Option B: Pure token bucket per tenant (rate limiting) with static caps
**Description:** Each tenant has a token bucket representing burst “budget” (e.g., burst GPU-seconds/s) with refill rate

selected for v1.

### Option B: Pure token bucket per tenant (rate limiting) with static caps
**Description:** Each tenant has a token bucket representing burst “budget” (e.g., burst GPU-seconds/s) with refill rate and burst size. Admit if tokens available.

**Pros**
- Simple, deterministic, low overhead.
- Easy to implement and test.
- Naturally produces explainable denials (“you exceeded your burst rate”).

**Cons / risks**
- Does not directly respond to pool-level contention. If every tenant is within its own budget, the pool can still overload.
- Does not guarantee fair sharing when the pool is saturated; whoever requests first may win.
- Can be too rigid for enterprise expectations (priority tiers).

**Conclusion:** Useful building block, but insufficient alone.

### Option C: Priority tiers only (gold/silver/standard), no per-tenant fairness
**Description:** Admit burst requests by tier; higher tier always wins until global caps hit.

**Pros**
- Simple product story.
- Easy to enforce “enterprise priority.”

**Cons / risks**
- Starvation risk for lower tiers during sustained saturation.
- Hard to measure and defend “fairness” within the same tier.
- Can create unpredictable customer experiences and elevated Support burden.

**Conclusion:** Not selected as a standalone solution.

### Option D (Selected): Tiered weighted token buckets + pool-level safety gates (with optional WFQ-style smoothing)
**Description:** Use hierarchical/tiered token buckets for fairness and enforce pool-level contention gates to prevent overload.

Core pieces:
1) **Tier weights** (e.g., gold > silver > standard) expressed as refill rates and/or maximum share.
2) **Per-tenant token bucket** within a tier to enforce fairness within that tier.
3) **Pool-level gates** (saturation, queue depth, telemetry lag, global fleet safety) to protect neighbors and SLOs.
4) **Deterministic decision function**: decision computed from a bounded set of inputs (tenant config + recent telemetry snapshot + current counters).

**Why this works:**
- Token buckets provide deterministic, explainable, rate-based fairness.
- Tiering supports packaging without making the scheduler fully preemptive.
- Pool-level gates ensure we never grant “fairly” into a meltdown.

## Decision
Adopt **Option D**: implement fairness as **tiered weighted token buckets** for burst admission, combined with **pool-level safety gates** and **anti-starvation constraints**.

This is the default and required fairness mechanism for all shared burst pools in v1.

## Detailed design
### Definitions
- **Baseline capacity**: tenant’s reserved Dedicated allocation (not part of burst pool fairness).
- **Burst request**: request that exceeds baseline capacity and must borrow from pool.
- **Burst unit for fairness accounting (v1)**: GPU-seconds (or GPU-milliseconds) attributed to the tenant’s incremental usage above baseline.
- **Tier**: configured priority class (standard, silver, gold). Tier impacts refill rates and maximum share.

### Hierarchical token bucket model
We model each pool with:
1) A **pool bucket** limiting total burst consumption (bounded by pool capacity

(standard, silver, gold). Tier impacts refill rates and maximum share.

### Hierarchical token bucket model
We model each pool with:
1) A **pool bucket** limiting total burst consumption (bounded by pool capacity and safety margin).
2) A **tier bucket** per tier (optional in v1, recommended; enables explicit tier shares).
3) A **tenant bucket** per tenant within tier.

Admission requires tokens from:
- pool bucket AND
- tenant bucket (and tier bucket if enabled)

If any bucket lacks tokens, deny (or queue, per ADR “admission control semantics”).

### Parameters (v1 defaults; configurable per pool)
All values below are expressed as guidance; exact numbers are set in pool config and can vary by region/hardware class.

1) **Max burst ratio (per tenant)**
- max_burst_ratio = 2.0 (tenant can burst up to 2x baseline capacity), subject to pool availability.

2) **Tenant token bucket**
- refill_rate: derived from baseline and tier weight.
- burst_size: allows short spikes (seconds to tens of seconds) without instant denial.
- cooldown_window: prevents oscillation when a tenant repeatedly hits cap.

3) **Tier weights**
- standard: 1.0
- silver: 1.5
- gold: 2.0

4) **Pool safety margin**
- reserve 10–20% of burst pool capacity as headroom to avoid tail latency blowups.

### Admission decision inputs (for determinism)
The admission controller decision MUST depend only on:
- Tenant config: tier, enablement, max_burst_ratio, explicit burst caps
- Pool config: capacity, safety margin, per-tier weights, max utilization, circuit breaker thresholds
- Telemetry snapshot: pool utilization, queue depth, p95/p99 latency deltas for non-burst tenants, telemetry freshness
- Controller counters: token balances and last refill timestamps

To avoid replica divergence:
- Token bucket refill uses monotonic time and quantized refill intervals (e.g., 100ms ticks).
- Decision is made against a single telemetry snapshot per request (timestamped).
- When telemetry freshness is outside the acceptable window, we fail closed to conservative gating (see Failure modes).

### Anti-starvation rules
To avoid starvation of smaller tenants within a tier:
- Tenant buckets include a minimum refill floor for enabled tenants (bounded by pool safety) so that low-volume tenants can occasionally burst even when a large tenant is continuously requesting.
- Enforce a maximum continuous-admission window per tenant under sustained saturation (implemented as a soft cap that increases deny probability/forces queueing).

### Denial reason mapping (supportability)
The admission controller returns a single primary denial reason code, stable over time:
- BURST_DISABLED
- TENANT_BURST_CAP_REACHED
- TENANT_COOLDOWN_ACTIVE
- POOL_SATURATED
- POOL_FLEET_SAFETY_CAP
- TIER_BUDGET_EXCEEDED
- TELEMETRY_STALE_FAILCLOSED
- CONTROLLER_OVERLOADED

These reason codes are expected to be surfaced in routing/gateway logs and customer-visible reporting.

## Measurable guardrails and success criteria
We will measure fairness and neighbor protection via:

1) **Per-tier share adherence**
- Metric: granted_burst_gpu_seconds_by_tier / total_granted_burst_gpu_seconds
- Goal: within ±10% of configured

and customer-visible reporting.

## Measurable guardrails and success criteria
We will measure fairness and neighbor protection via:

1) **Per-tier share adherence**
- Metric: granted_burst_gpu_seconds_by_tier / total_granted_burst_gpu_seconds
- Goal: within ±10% of configured tier weights during sustained saturation (over 15m windows).

2) **Within-tier fairness**
- Metric: Jain’s fairness index over tenants’ granted_burst_gpu_seconds (computed per tier, per pool, per 15m window).
- Goal: ≥ 0.85 in load tests; ≥ 0.75 in production (allowing real-world burstiness).

3) **Starvation rate**
- Metric: percentage of enabled tenants with > N consecutive denials while pool has non-zero grants.
- Goal: < 1% for N=50 within 15m windows.

4) **Neighbor impact (non-burst protection)**
- Metrics:
  - nonburst_p95_latency_delta (vs baseline period)
  - tail_amplification_ratio (p99/p50)
  - error_rate for non-burst tenants
- Goal: No sustained regression beyond SLO gates; triggers automatic reduction/disable of burst when exceeded.

5) **Determinism / stability**
- Metric: retry_admit_flip_rate (same request idempotency key sees admit/deny flip within a short window)
- Goal: near-zero except during config changes.

## Failure modes and fallback behavior
1) **Telemetry lag / stale telemetry**
- Behavior: fail closed for pool-level gates (deny or queue with conservative limits), return TELEMETRY_STALE_FAILCLOSED.
- Rationale: better to deny burst than to risk fleet-wide tail latency.

2) **Controller overload**
- Behavior: shed load, return CONTROLLER_OVERLOADED; routing should apply exponential backoff and/or fallback per admission semantics ADR.

3) **Hot pool / tail latency regression**
- Behavior: trigger pool circuit breaker (deny new burst admissions), allow existing bursts to drain, surface POOL_SATURATED or POOL_FLEET_SAFETY_CAP.

4) **Tier misconfiguration**
- Behavior: defaults to standard tier weight; audit log required for tier changes.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Deterministic and supportable: denial reasons map directly to one of a small number of gates/buckets.
- Measurable fairness with explicit KPIs and dashboards.
- Supports packaging (tiers) without requiring complex distributed queuing.

### Negative / trade-offs
- Token bucket fairness is time-based and may not perfectly approximate instantaneous fairness under extremely bursty workloads.
- Requires careful calibration of token units (GPU-seconds) and refill rates to match real consumption.
- Some customers may expect “gold always wins”; we explicitly avoid absolute starvation of lower tiers.

## Rollout plan
1) Implement token bucket fairness in admission controller with standard tier only (no tier buckets), validate determinism.
2) Enable tier weights for limited beta tenants; validate share adherence and anti-starvation metrics.
3) Add tier buckets (if needed) for stricter tier share enforcement under saturation.
4) GA: enforce fairness model for all shared pools; disallow per-tenant bespoke scheduling logic.

Rollout guard: error-budget / SLO gate can automatically reduce or disable burst in a region/hardware class if non-burst latency regresses beyond configured thresholds.

## Security and audit
- Tier changes, burst enable/disable, and cap updates MUST

SLO gate can automatically reduce or disable burst in a region/hardware class if non-burst latency regresses beyond configured thresholds.

## Security and audit
- Tier changes, burst enable/disable, and cap updates MUST be audit logged.
- Support tooling can view decision explanations with redaction (no cross-tenant identifiers beyond hashed tenant id).

## Open questions
1) Should we standardize fairness accounting on GPU-seconds only, or incorporate token-level throughput as a secondary constraint (model-dependent)?
2) Do we need separate tier weights per pool (region/hardware class) for procurement-driven constraints?
3) What is the long-term stance on “enterprise override” during incidents (manual priority boosts), and how do we bound blast radius?

## Appendix: Why we did not choose pure WFQ
We do not have a single serialized queue per pool; routing is distributed and admission happens concurrently. Implementing WFQ with strong determinism would require additional shared state, ordering guarantees, or a central coordinator—adding latency, complexity, and failure modes. Token buckets provide a safer, more deterministic first implementation while still enabling measurable fairness and tiering.

Service Chain SLO Allocation and Enforcement (ADR) — 2026

Overview:

This ADR documents the chosen approach for allocating, enforcing, and monitoring SLO budgets across multi-service inference request chains. It standardizes how we decompose end-to-end SLOs into per-service targets, the telemetry and enforcement knobs required at each hop, and a migration plan for existing services.

Context and problem statement:

- Redwood serves composite inference requests frequently: client -> frontend -> routing -> model-router -> model-shard -> postprocessor -> metrics. Each hop contributes latency and error risk.
- Many current incidents arise when one intermediate service exceeds its latency budget, cascading and causing the entire chain to violate the customer-visible SLO. We lack a uniform, machine-readable allocation strategy and enforcement surface.
- Teams currently apply ad-hoc allocations in design docs, which causes inconsistent telemetry labels, uncoordinated fallbacks, and uneven customer experience.

Goals:

1. Provide a reproducible formula to split end-to-end SLOs into per-hop budgets that accounts for variability and retry amplification.
2. Define a lightweight enforcement contract (request headers, tokens, and local circuit rules) that all services implement.
3. Establish telemetry and alerting requirements so SRE/Owners can diagnose chain-level violations rapidly.
4. Support graceful degradation strategies: canary fallback to lower-cost quantized variants, partial response, and queued retries.
5. Ensure backward-compatibility for services that cannot implement the full enforcement contract immediately.

Decision summary:

We adopt a two-layer allocation + enforcement strategy:

A. Allocation: the end-to-end SLO is decomposed using a headroom and amplification model into deterministic per-hop budgets.
- Headroom H (ms) reserves time for unexpected jitter and network variance.
- Amplification factor A accounts for expected retries and client-side backoff behavior.
- Each hop i receives budget B_i = max(min_alloc, floor((E2E_SLO - H) * W_i / sum(W) / A)) where W_i is the hop weight reflecting expected mean compute time.

B. Enforcement: service-level local enforcers apply these budgets using:
- request context headers: X-RW-SLO-ID, X-RW-E2E-SLO-ms, X-RW-REM-BUDGET-ms, X-RW-HINTS (json-encoded client hints).
- budget tokens: a per-request remaining_budget value passed downstream; services decrement before local scheduling and can reject/short-circuit when remaining_budget < local_min_cutoff.
- soft and hard limits: soft_limit triggers adaptive degradation, hard_limit forces a controlled abort and counted error.

Trade-offs considered:

- Centralized vs distributed allocation: centralized (API Gateway computes concrete B_i) simplifies consistency but creates a single point of failure and additional latency. Distributed (each service computes weights W_i from a shared registry) reduces central coupling but needs strong versioning of weight tables. We chose a hybrid: gateway issues allocation when present; otherwise services compute deterministic B_i from registry.
- Strict enforcement vs graceful defaults: strict enforcement minimizes customer-visible SLA misses but can harm availability. We chose a two-tier enforcement (soft degrade then hard abort) to balance availability and correctness.

Specification (required fields and behaviors):

1) Request header contract (all services must support reading these headers; writing is optional unless the service is an allocation point):
-

then hard abort) to balance availability and correctness.

Specification (required fields and behaviors):

1) Request header contract (all services must support reading these headers; writing is optional unless the service is an allocation point):
- X-RW-SLO-ID: string (uuid)
- X-RW-E2E-SLO-ms: integer (ms)
- X-RW-REM-BUDGET-ms: integer (ms) — remaining budget when the request arrives
- X-RW-ALLOCATION-VERSION: string (semver of registry weights)
- X-RW-HINTS: base64(json) (optional client hints: max_tokens, prefer_low_cost_variant)

2) Allocation algorithm (pseudocode)
- Inputs: E2E_SLO, H, A, weight_table W[1..N], min_alloc (default 5ms)
- Step 1: available = max(E2E_SLO - H, min_total)
- Step 2: for i in hops: B_i = max(min_alloc, floor(available * W_i / sum(W) / A))
- Step 3: Gateway attaches B_i for first M hops or writes X-RW-REM-BUDGET = E2E_SLO - H to allow downstream deterministic calculation

3) Enforcement semantics
- On receive: read X-RW-REM-BUDGET (if missing assume E2E_SLO - H), compute local_budget = allocated or derived B_i
- If local_estimated_latency > local_budget * soft_threshold (0.8) -> trigger degrade path (quantized model, reduced context length, drop expensive re-rank) and emit metric slo.local.soft_degrade=1
- If local_estimated_latency > local_budget * hard_threshold (1.0) -> abort with standardized error HTTP 507 (Insufficient Time) and reason header X-RW-ABORT-REASON

4) Telemetry and SLI requirements (mandatory)
- Metrics (per-service, per-route): e2e_slo_ms, rem_budget_on_arrival_ms, local_budget_ms, p50/p95/p99 latency_ms, local.soft_degrade_count, local.hard_abort_count, retries_initiated_count
- Traces: every request MUST propagate X-RW-SLO-ID as trace tag. All spans should record rem_budget_on_start and rem_budget_on_exit.
- Logs: when soft_degrade or hard_abort occurs, log structured record with fields {slo_id, route, rem_budget_on_arrival_ms, local_budget_ms, decision, variant_chosen}.

5) Alerting thresholds (suggested defaults)
- Per-route: >1% hard_abort_count over 5m AND p95 latency > allocated budget -> P0/Immediate paged alert to owning SRE team.
- Per-service: soft_degrade_ratio >10% over 15m -> P1 notify.

Operational playbook (runbook summary):

1) Detection: automated alert triggers.
2) Initial triage: look at slo_id trace for failed requests and compare rem_budget_on_arrival across hops.
3) If root cause is upstream amplification (retries/backoff), escalate to routing owners and consider adjusting A in weight registry.
4) If a single shard shows high p95 but low p50, schedule kernel-level profiling and check continuity of KV cache hit rates.

Migration and compatibility

- Pilot rollout (4 weeks):
  1. Select non-critical staging routes behind feature flag.
  2. Gateway populates full allocation headers for pilot traffic.
  3. Collect metrics and traces; refine weight_table W and H.

- Gradual rollout (tiered):
  - Phase 1: Gateway-only allocations (no downstream enforcement) — 2 weeks
  - Phase 2: Deploy header-reading and soft_degrade behavior to critical services — 3 weeks
  - Phase 3: Enable hard abort enforcement behind kill-switch — 2 weeks
  - Phase 4: Full enforcement on all traffic for team-owned services — ongoing

- Central switch: SRE can toggle global rw.slo.enforcement.disable via feature-flagging platform — this sets gateway to stop writing allocations and services to ignore enforcement.

Testing and verification

- Unit tests: allocation math, header parsing, and local decision logic.
- Integration tests: synthetic chains in the perf harness with injected jitter and retries. Verify that when one hop fails, soft_degrade triggers at downstream hops and that hard_abort preserves clear error semantics.
- Load test: run 72-hour simulated traffic with mixed QPS and measure that p95 chain latency meets E2E SLO for 99% of intervals.

ADR: Proactive Eviction Signal and Priority Decay for Multi-tenant GPU Scheduling

Summary

This ADR describes a standard for emitting a proactive-eviction signal and applying a tunable priority-decay policy across Redwood's multi-tenant GPU serving pools. The goal is to reduce sudden, high-impact preemptions and to provide deterministic, SLO-aware behavior during resource contention and node degradations.

Context and motivation

Problem: Sudden GPU preemptions and uncoordinated evictions have produced high tail-latency and user-visible failures for customers on Dedicated and Private deployments. The existing eviction policy is reactive (kill lowest-priority pods when OOM or preemption occurs), which causes wide variance in request latencies and complicates cache affinity.

Requirements driving the decision:
- Minimize 99.9th percentile latency impact during capacity pressure.
- Provide predictable, debuggable behavior for tenants (clear signals in telemetry).
- Allow graceful degradation and partial progress for long-running streaming/partial-result requests.
- Be compatible with existing model-variant fallback and routing policies.

Non-goals:
- This ADR does not redefine autoscaling or cluster sizing; it is an eviction and priority policy used during transient contention.

Decision

We will implement a two-part mechanism: (1) a proactive-eviction signal emitted by node and job-level probes when heuristics indicate imminent resource exhaustion, and (2) a priority-decay algorithm applied to tenant queues and job tokens so that lower-importance work gracefully reduces its resource share over a configurable decay window.

Key components:
- ProactiveEvictSignal (node-agent): a node-local event emitted when combination of metrics (GPU memory pressure > 85% sustained for 4s OR GPU SM saturation > 95% for 1s with growing queue length) is observed. The signal is propagated to the regional scheduler via the control plane event bus with structured metadata (node-id, metric-snapshot, timestamp, probe-version).
- PriorityDecayController (scheduler): when the signal is received, the scheduler starts applying a decay multiplier to per-tenant priorities. The decay is proportional to the severity score (see scoring below) and bounded by configured min/max multipliers.
- Tenant affordance: each tenant request has a priority_class (critical|high|normal|best_effort) and a time-to-degrade (TTD) attribute set by the client SDK or default server policy. PriorityDecayController respects priority_class ceilings and does not decay critical below 0.6 multiplier.

Severity scoring (simplified):
- severity = clamp(0,1, (mem_util_norm * 0.6) + (sm_util_norm * 0.3) + (queue_growth_factor * 0.1))
- mem_util_norm = (mem_used - mem_threshold) / (1 - mem_threshold) where mem_threshold = 0.85
- sm_util_norm = (sm_util - 0.95)/(1 - 0.95)
- queue_growth_factor = sigmoid(normalized_recent_queue_delta)

Operational knobs (defaults):
| setting | default | meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| proactive_signal_window | 4s | minimum sustained window for memory pressure probe |
| mem_pressure_threshold | 0.85 | fraction of GPU memory used to start scoring |
| decay_base | 0.9 | multiplier applied per decay step |
| decay_step_ms | 500 | scheduler step interval for progressive decay |
| decay_min_multiplier | 0.2 | absolute lower bound for non-critical classes |
| critical_min_multiplier | 0.6 | lower bound for critical priority_class |

Consequences and rationale

Positive consequences:
- Smoother

scheduler step interval for progressive decay |
| decay_min_multiplier | 0.2 | absolute lower bound for non-critical classes |
| critical_min_multiplier | 0.6 | lower bound for critical priority_class |

Consequences and rationale

Positive consequences:
- Smoother degradation: long-running requests observe gradual priority reduction rather than immediate termination.
- More predictable SLOs: telemetry will show a progressive shift in qps distribution instead of spikes of failures.
- Better cache affinity preservation: by avoiding mass kills we retain warmed KV caches on nodes longer.

Risks and mitigations:
- Complexity: adding another control-plane signal increases surface area. Mitigation: start with conservative defaults, feature-flag the mechanism, and add strong observability (see rollout plan).
- Starvation of best_effort workloads may last longer than intended. Mitigation: decay windows have max-duration and automatic reset when severity subsides.

Rollout plan and telemetry

Phased rollout:
1) Canary (2 clusters): enable the ProactiveEvictSignal in read-only mode — signals emitted but ignored. Collect telemetry to validate thresholds and false-positive rate for 2 weeks.
2) Soft-apply (10% capacity): enable PriorityDecayController with gentle decay_base=0.98 and short windows; enable only for best_effort class. Monitor request error rate, p99 latency, and cache-miss rate for 4 weeks.
3) Full-apply (100%): enable default configuration globally after 30 days of stable metrics.

Telemetry to capture (minimum):
- proactive_evict_events.count by node, severity histogram
- priority_multiplier.time_series per-tenant and per-priority_class
- request_outcomes (success, partial, aborted) with tags: tenant, priority_class, decay_multiplier
- p50/p95/p99 latency delta before/after signal window
- cache_warmth_retention metric to confirm affinity preservation

Runbook excerpt (quick actions for SRE):
1. Identify recent proactive_evict_events for node X:
   kubectl -n infra logs node-agent-X | grep ProactiveEvict
2. If false positives are high, temporarily increase mem_pressure_threshold:
   curl -X POST https://control-plane/api/v1/node-probes/config -d '{"mem_pressure_threshold":0.9}'
3. To disable PriorityDecayController cluster-wide: set feature-flag: "priority_decay.enabled=false" in config service and restart scheduler: systemctl restart rwd-scheduler

Configuration example (YAML)

# Example config for regional scheduler
scheduler:
  priority_decay:
    enabled: true
    decay_base: 0.9
    decay_step_ms: 500
    decay_min_multiplier: 0.25
    critical_min_multiplier: 0.6

Appendix: example severity calculation (Python)

```python
import math

def clamp(x, a=0.0, b=1.0):
    return max(a, min(b, x))

def severity(mem_used, sm_util, queue_delta_norm):
    mem_threshold = 0.85
    mem_norm = clamp((mem_used - mem_threshold) / (1 - mem_threshold))
    sm_norm = clamp((sm_util - 0.95) / (1 - 0.95))
    queue_factor = 1/(1+math.exp(-queue_delta_norm))
    raw = mem_norm*0.6 + sm_norm*0.3 + queue_factor*0.1
    return clamp(raw)
```

ADR-007: Standard KMS Client Wrapper and Failure Policy

## Status
Published.

## Summary
We will standardize all Key Management Service (KMS/HSM-backed) calls in the Redwood monorepo behind a shared **KMS client wrapper** with:
- Explicit, consistent **timeouts** and **retry budgets** (with jitter/backoff).
- A canonical **error taxonomy** used across logs, metrics, traces, and user-facing/operator-facing messages.
- A shared **circuit breaker** and **backpressure** policy to prevent retry storms and cascading failures when KMS is degraded.
- Strict **caching constraints** and safe defaults appropriate for envelope encryption.

This ADR defines the wrapper API shape, failure-handling rules, observability requirements, and non-goals.

## Context / Problem
Redwood’s Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments all integrate with customer-managed KMS/HSM for envelope encryption flows (e.g., DEK generation/encryption, DEK decryption, key metadata lookups).

Prior to this ADR, KMS interactions differed across services (control plane vs data plane), leading to:
- Inconsistent timeouts and SDK default retries (often too aggressive) causing **tail latency** and **retry amplification**.
- Non-uniform error handling (e.g., throttling treated as generic 500s) which increased time-to-triage.
- Missing or inconsistent telemetry (no shared tag set; inconsistent metric names).
- Confusing operator experiences (unclear “AccessDenied” vs wrong key ARN vs key disabled).

We also experienced a near-miss retry storm during a regional timeout spike where client retries amplified load on KMS and increased 5xx rates.

## Goals
1) Provide a single, reviewed integration point for KMS calls with safe defaults.
2) Ensure predictable latency behavior via explicit timeouts + bounded retries.
3) Improve triage and post-incident analysis via a canonical taxonomy + telemetry.
4) Prevent cascading failures via circuit breakers and backpressure.
5) Establish guardrails so services cannot silently override safety-critical defaults without an explicit, audited override.

## Non-goals
- Introducing new cryptographic primitives or changing algorithms.
- Building a “KMS proxy” service or sidecar as part of this initiative.
- Implementing a universal key rotation workflow (see ADR-008).
- Persistently caching plaintext key material or storing decrypted DEKs outside process memory.

## Decision
### Decision 1: All KMS calls must go through a shared wrapper library
We will implement and mandate a shared wrapper library (e.g., `redwood/kmsclient`) used by:
- Control plane services that manage key references and encryption configuration.
- Data plane services that decrypt/encrypt envelope payloads.
- Private installer/validator components that perform preflight KMS checks.

Direct usage of cloud provider SDK KMS clients in production services is disallowed unless an exception is approved (see Key Management Standard / exceptions process).

### Decision 2: Establish a canonical error taxonomy
All errors surfaced by the wrapper are mapped into a small set of canonical error categories with stable semantics.

#### Canonical error categories
| Category | Examples | Retry? | Severity / Notes |

surfaced by the wrapper are mapped into a small set of canonical error categories with stable semantics.

#### Canonical error categories
| Category | Examples | Retry? | Severity / Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `KMS_ACCESS_DENIED` | IAM denies, missing `Decrypt`, wrong principal | No | Actionable operator error; include missing permission and key identifier if available. |
| `KMS_NOT_FOUND` | key ID/ARN/alias not found, wrong region, deleted key | No | Actionable; often config error. |
| `KMS_INVALID_CIPHERTEXT` | ciphertext invalid, wrong key version, corrupted payload | No | Usually indicates key mismatch or data corruption; triggers incident workflow depending on scope. |
| `KMS_KEY_DISABLED` | key disabled/pending deletion | No | Actionable; can block all decrypt; escalate to customer/security immediately. |
| `KMS_THROTTLED` | provider quota exceeded, `ThrottlingException`, 429 | Yes (bounded) | Retry with exponential backoff + jitter; enforce throttle budget. |
| `KMS_TIMEOUT` | request deadline exceeded | Yes (bounded) | Retry only within total budget; feed into circuit breaker. |
| `KMS_TRANSIENT` | 5xx, connection reset, temporary DNS | Yes (bounded) | Retry with jitter; feed into circuit breaker. |
| `KMS_MISCONFIGURED` | invalid key ARN format, unsupported region, missing endpoint in Private | No | Fail fast at startup/preflight where possible. |
| `KMS_UNKNOWN` | unclassified | Maybe (bounded) | Treated as transient only if clearly network/5xx; otherwise no retry. |

#### Requirements for error payloads
The wrapper must attach structured fields consistently:
- `kms.provider` (aws|gcp|azure)
- `kms.operation` (Decrypt|Encrypt|GenerateDataKey|GetKey|GetKeyPolicy|…)
- `kms.key_ref` (redacted/hashed if customer-sensitive; never log plaintext secrets)
- `kms.region`
- `error.category` (canonical)
- `error.code` (provider code if present)
- `retry.attempt` and `retry.exhausted` (boolean)
- `circuit.state` (closed|open|half_open)

### Decision 3: Timeouts and retry budgets are explicit and bounded
We will not rely on cloud SDK defaults.

#### Default timeout and retry policy (safe defaults)
All values below are defaults; services may tighten them (stricter) without approval. Loosening them requires an explicit override with Security + SRE review.

| Operation | Default per-attempt timeout | Max attempts | Total time budget (cap) | Retry on |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `Decrypt` | 750ms | 2 | 1.5s | `KMS_THROTTLED`, `KMS_TIMEOUT`, `KMS_TRANSIENT` |
| `Encrypt` | 750ms | 2 | 1.5s | `KMS_THROTTLED`, `KMS_TIMEOUT`, `KMS_TRANSIENT` |
| `GenerateDataKey` | 1.0s | 2 | 2.0s | `KMS_THROTTLED`, `KMS_TIMEOUT`, `KMS_TRANSIENT` |
| `GetKeyMetadata` / key lookup | 500ms | 2 | 1.0s | `KMS_THROTTLED`, `KMS_TIMEOUT`, `KMS_TRANSIENT` |

Backoff: exponential with full jitter.
- Initial delay: 50ms
- Max delay: 300ms
- Jitter: required
- Respect `Retry-After` where provided (bounded by total time budget)

Retry is explicitly disabled for non-retryable categories (`KMS_ACCESS_DENIED`, `KMS_NOT_FOUND`, `KMS_INVALID_CIPHERTEXT`, `KMS_KEY_DISABLED`, `KMS_MISCONFIGURED`).

### Decision 4: Add a shared circuit breaker and backpressure policy
We will implement

provided (bounded by total time budget)

Retry is explicitly disabled for non-retryable categories (`KMS_ACCESS_DENIED`, `KMS_NOT_FOUND`, `KMS_INVALID_CIPHERTEXT`, `KMS_KEY_DISABLED`, `KMS_MISCONFIGURED`).

### Decision 4: Add a shared circuit breaker and backpressure policy
We will implement a circuit breaker per (provider, region, operation) with a conservative default to prevent request storms.

#### Circuit breaker semantics
- **Closed:** normal operation; collect rolling metrics.
- **Open:** fail fast with a typed error (`KMS_DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE`) without calling KMS.
- **Half-open:** allow a limited number of probe requests to test recovery.

#### Default breaker thresholds
(Subject to tuning during rollout; changes require SRE review.)
- Rolling window: 60s
- Minimum request volume before evaluation: 50
- Open breaker if either:
  - Failure rate >= 20% for retryable categories (`KMS_TIMEOUT`, `KMS_TRANSIENT`, `KMS_THROTTLED`) OR
  - Consecutive timeouts >= 25
- Open duration: 30s (then half-open)
- Half-open probe rate: max 1 req/s per key (provider/region/operation)

#### Backpressure (throttle budget)
When `KMS_THROTTLED` is observed, the wrapper will apply a token-bucket-style throttle budget per (provider, region, operation) to avoid saturating KMS under load spikes. If budget is exhausted, the wrapper fails fast with `KMS_THROTTLED` and `retry.exhausted=true` rather than attempting additional retries.

### Decision 5: Caching is allowed only for metadata and short-lived in-memory key material, with strict constraints
Because we are using envelope encryption, caching can reduce KMS load but must not expand the blast radius of key compromise.

#### Allowed caches
1) **Key metadata cache** (safe):
- Examples: alias → key ARN, key state, supported algorithms
- TTL default: 1 hour
- Negative cache TTL (not found): 60 seconds
- Must be invalidated on rotation/config change events where applicable.

2) **In-memory DEK/plaintext key material cache** (restricted):
- Allowed only for plaintext DEKs that are already present in memory for request processing.
- TTL default: 5 minutes (configurable downwards)
- Max entries: service-specific but must be bounded (default 10,000 entries) with LRU eviction.
- Scope: in-process only; never persisted; never shared cross-host.
- Must not include raw customer identifiers in cache keys (use hashed stable identifiers).
- Must be disable-able via config in regulated environments.

#### Disallowed caches
- Persisting plaintext DEKs (disk, database, distributed cache).
- Long-lived plaintext caches (> 15 minutes) without a security exception.
- Caching ciphertext blobs in a way that bypasses key version validation or rotation safeguards.

## Rationale
- **Consistency + safety:** A single wrapper ensures safe defaults and reduces per-team re-implementation risk.
- **Reliability:** Explicit deadlines and a circuit breaker prevent KMS incidents from becoming platform-wide outages due to retry amplification.
- **Observability:** Canonical taxonomy and stable fields enable dashboards/alerts/runbooks that work across all deployments.
- **Enterprise readiness:** Actionable errors and documented behavior are required for regulated customers and security reviews.

## Detailed Design

**Observability:** Canonical taxonomy and stable fields enable dashboards/alerts/runbooks that work across all deployments.
- **Enterprise readiness:** Actionable errors and documented behavior are required for regulated customers and security reviews.

## Detailed Design Notes
### Wrapper API (language-agnostic contract)
The wrapper must expose an interface roughly equivalent to:
- `Encrypt(ctx, keyRef, plaintext, opts)`
- `Decrypt(ctx, keyRef, ciphertext, opts)`
- `GenerateDataKey(ctx, keyRef, opts)`
- `GetKeyMetadata(ctx, keyRef, opts)`

Where `opts` includes:
- `deadline` (optional; defaults applied if absent)
- `idempotency_key` (where supported/needed)
- `cache_policy` (metadata-only; allow/deny in-memory DEK cache)
- `telemetry_context` (service name, environment, deployment mode)

### Telemetry requirements
Metrics (names are illustrative; final names must follow observability standards):
- `kms.client.request_latency_ms` (histogram) with tags: provider, region, operation, deployment_mode, service
- `kms.client.errors_total` (counter) with tags: provider, region, operation, error.category, error.code
- `kms.client.retries_total` (counter) with tags: provider, region, operation
- `kms.client.circuit_open_total` (counter) with tags: provider, region, operation
- `kms.client.cache_hits_total` / `kms.client.cache_misses_total` (counter) with tags: cache_type

Tracing:
- A span per KMS call with attributes matching the structured fields listed above.
- Errors must be recorded on the span with canonical error category.

Logging:
- Log at WARN for retryable failures when retries are exhausted.
- Log at ERROR for non-retryable categories and for circuit breaker opens.
- Never log plaintext key material or decrypted DEKs.

### Failure policy by component type
We explicitly distinguish between:
- **Data-plane decrypt path:** If decrypt fails, the request fails. The wrapper’s job is to fail quickly and consistently under KMS degradation, not to silently bypass encryption.
- **Control-plane metadata/config:** Prefer fail fast on misconfiguration (preflight validation, startup checks). For transient KMS errors, allow bounded retries but do not block entire control-plane reconciliation loops beyond the global time budget.
- **Installer/preflight (Private):** Must provide actionable diagnostics and an exportable validation report. Retries may be higher in preflight mode (since it is operator-driven), but still bounded.

## Alternatives Considered
1) **Do nothing / per-service KMS clients**
- Rejected: inconsistent timeouts/retries/telemetry; repeated mistakes; higher incident risk.

2) **Rely on cloud provider SDK default retries/timeouts**
- Rejected: defaults vary by language/provider; often tuned for throughput not tail latency; risk of retry storms.

3) **Service mesh / network-level retries**
- Rejected: cannot classify KMS-specific error codes well; may retry non-idempotent operations incorrectly; obscures metrics.

4) **Central KMS proxy service**
- Deferred: could improve policy enforcement and caching, but adds a new dependency and availability concerns; out of scope for this quarter.

5) **Adopt a third-party library as-is (e.g., generic KMS wrappers)**
- Rejected: insufficient support for Redwood’s deployment modes, telemetry conventions, and failure policy requirements; would still require significant customization.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Reduced risk of cascading failures during KMS degradation.
- Better on-call ergonomics and faster triage due to

conventions, and failure policy requirements; would still require significant customization.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Reduced risk of cascading failures during KMS degradation.
- Better on-call ergonomics and faster triage due to consistent taxonomy and fields.
- Easier security reviews and documentation consistency across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.

### Negative / Tradeoffs
- Slight increase in shared-library coupling; wrapper changes require careful rollout.
- Conservative time budgets may increase request failures during severe KMS degradation; this is an explicit tradeoff to protect overall platform availability and prevent retry amplification.

## Rollout Plan
1) Implement wrapper with feature flags and dual instrumentation.
2) Migrate highest-risk call sites first (data-plane decrypt/encrypt).
3) Enforce guardrails:
   - Lints / codeowners for direct SDK usage.
   - CI checks that require wrapper usage in approved services.
4) Roll out by environment (dev → staging → prod) with SRE-defined canary criteria:
   - No increase in 5xx beyond error budget threshold.
   - No increase in P99 latency beyond agreed guardrails.
   - Circuit breaker open rate within expected bounds.
5) Post-rollout review and tuning of thresholds.

## Security & Compliance Notes
- Logging must avoid customer-sensitive identifiers where feasible; prefer hashed or redacted key references.
- Overrides that loosen retry/timeouts or extend key material caching require documented approval (Security + SRE) and must be auditable.
- This ADR aligns with the Key Management Standard; any deviations require an exception request.

## Open Questions
- Provider-specific nuances for Azure Key Vault throttling and recommended retry headers (tracked in implementation tickets).
- Whether certain metadata calls can be consolidated and cached more aggressively without compromising correctness during rotation (coordinate with ADR-008).

ADR: Metric ownership, volatility mitigation, and consumer contracts

Summary

This ADR establishes a company-wide contract for metric ownership, defines mitigation patterns for metric volatility, and specifies the consumer contract for downstream telemetry users (dashboards, alerting, SLI evaluators, billing). The intent is to reduce alert noise, avoid SLO churn due to metric instability, and make metric responsibilities and lifecycle explicit.

Context

Problem statements we observed in Q4 2025 and Q1 2026:
- Dashboards show repeated spikes in the same metrics after infra rollouts, leading to noisy alerts and paging.
- Teams create ad-hoc metrics with conflicting names/semantics.
- Automated SLI producers and billing pipelines behave differently when metric cardinality or labels change, causing incorrect cost allocation.
- Backfills and metric renames often regress the availability of historical SLI evidence.

Goals
- Make metric producers accountable and discoverable.
- Reduce consumer-facing volatility (noise and SLO destabilization).
- Provide a standard contract so observability consumers can rely on stability guarantees and failure modes.

Decision (high level)

1) Metric ownership: every metric must have an explicit owner and metadata. Metadata keys required: producer-service, metric-description, unit, owner-email, cardinality-bound, stability-tier, created-via (code-review/auto). Ownership is the responsibility of the owning service team.

2) Stability tiers: metrics are assigned one of three stability tiers at creation:
   - stable: semantically fixed and backward-compatible. Allowed to be used by SLI/Billing/Customer-facing dashboards.
   - experimental: allowed in internal dashboards and alerting only with guardrails. Not allowed for long-term SLI/Billing.
   - deprecated: read-only alias pointing to a successor; expected removal timeline present.

3) Volatility mitigation patterns: recommended mitigations for high-cardinality or bursty metrics:
   - cardinality-bound enforcement (reject or sample labels beyond N unique values per minute).
   - reservoir sampling and percentile smoothing with explicit retention of raw counters for debug windows.
   - aggregated and rollup metrics with stable label sets.
   - circuit-breaker for metric emission: when a producer notices cardinality blowup, it should switch to a summarized/aggregated emission mode and emit a special metric (metric.production_mode = "aggregated") to signal consumers.

4) Consumer contract: consumers (alerting, SLI evaluation, billing) must declare which stability tiers they accept. By default:
   - SLI evaluation: stable only.
   - Billing and chargeback: stable only.
   - Internal dashboards: stable + experimental (with a per-team exception).
   - Synthetic tests and canary analysis jobs: experimental allowed but must include provenance metadata.

5) Schema and metadata: metrics must be registered in the central Metric Registry (see Implementation). Registration requires a JSON manifest with required keys (see Appendix). Attempts to use non-registered metrics in SLI rules will auto-fail CI lint.

Consequences

Positive:
- Fewer unexpected SLO regressions caused by metric renames and unbounded cardinality.
- Clear escalation path for noisy metrics: contact owner -> throttling -> temporary circuit -> deprecation.

Positive:
- Fewer unexpected SLO regressions caused by metric renames and unbounded cardinality.
- Clear escalation path for noisy metrics: contact owner -> throttling -> temporary circuit -> deprecation.

Trade-offs and work required:
- Upfront overhead for teams to register metrics and add metadata.
- Some historical dashboards and scripts will need migration to registered metric names or aliases.

Implementation (step-by-step)

Owner: Observability Platform (eng-platform) + Metrics Guild representatives.

1) Metric Registry service (MRS): a lightweight service and git-backed catalog (YAML/JSON). Fields required: name, description, producer_service, owner_email, unit, stability_tier, cardinality_bound, schema_version, created_at, notes. The registry exposes an API and a CLI for registration.

2) CI Lint rule: a linter plugin for service repositories that checks for metric registration during PRs. The linter enforces naming conventions (kebab_case with service prefix) and presence of metadata. Example CI check failure message will include remediation steps.

3) Runtime producer SDK changes: open-source SDKs ingest a registry token and enforce cardinality bounds and emission modes. SDKs will emit extra diagnostic metrics when mitigation is triggered: metric.camel_case_protection_throttle_total, metric.cardinality_change_events.

4) Consumer changes: SLI evaluation pipeline will require a single config key (accepted_stability_tiers) per SLI rule. Dashboard templates will show metric stability and link to owner contact. Alerting playbooks will include a triage procedure tied to owner metadata.

5) Observability platform automation: automated email/Slack alert to owner after a metric crosses volatility thresholds (e.g., 3x median cardinality or > 10% error increase correlated with spikes).

Migration plan

1) Phase 0 (30 days): Publish registry schema, sample manifests, CI linter plugin alpha. Invite pilot teams (Runtime, Serving-runtime, SRE) to register top 200 metrics.

2) Phase 1 (60 days): SDK updates released (backwards compatible) and canary plugin applied to 25% of repos. Alerting consumers begin to require stability_tier on new SLI rules.

3) Phase 2 (90–180 days): Enforce registration in PRs for all teams (blocking). SLI/billing pipelines reject unregistered metrics for new SLI definitions. Run a migration sweep to map legacy names to registry aliases.

4) Decommission window (180–360 days): Deprecation policy enforced. Deprecated metrics maintained as read-only aliases for at least 180 days with telemetry backfill available on request.

Monitoring and SLOs for the ADR itself

We will track the rollout and effectiveness with the following measures:
- percent_metrics_registered (goal > 90% top 500 metrics within 120 days)
- metric_noise_rate (defined as alerts triggered by metric volatility patterns; goal reduce by 40% in 6 months)
- SLI_stability_incidents (number of SLI regressions traced to metric changes; target 0 after 6 months)

Rollback plan
